items.text: A session is one conversation between a user and the agent, from when the chat is opened until it ends. Today, the agent does not manage sessions: there is no clear way to identify a conversation, continue it later, continue it on another device, or clean up old ones.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
The feature organizes conversations into sessions:

  • Gives each session a unique ID and tracks it.
  • Synchronizes the same session across devices.
  • Ends inactive sessions and cleans up temporary data.
  • Lets users resume a session where they left off.
  • Lets the team monitor active sessions.

items.title: Example
items.text:
The user starts a conversation on her phone, asking about a vitamin C serum. Later, she opens GoCare on her laptop and finds the same conversation, and continues from where she stopped.

If she leaves the chat for a long time, the session is closed automatically, and its temporary data is cleaned up.

items.title: 2. Why It Matters
items.text:
• Continuity: users do not lose their conversation when they change devices or close the page.
  • Organized data: every message belongs to a clear session and user.
  • Server health: inactive sessions are cleaned up, saving resources.
  • Foundation for memory: Conversation Memory Management needs sessions to know which messages belong together.

items.title: Functional Requirements
items.text:
• FR-01: Session identification and tracking: each session has a unique ID linked to a user, with start time, last activity, and status.
  • FR-02: Multi-device synchronization: a logged-in user can continue the same session on different devices.
  • FR-03: Session timeout and cleanup: inactive sessions are closed after a set time, and temporary data is cleaned up.
  • FR-04: Session resume: users can reopen and continue a previous session.
  • FR-05: Active session monitoring: the team can see the number and status of active sessions.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
• Security: session IDs must not be guessable, and users can only access their own sessions.
  • Performance: creating and loading sessions must be fast.
  • Scalability: sessions must work across multiple agent instances.
  • Reliability: an expired or invalid session must be handled gracefully, for example by starting a new one.

items.title: 4. Technical Approach
items.text:
• Session store: store sessions in a shared database or cache, such as Redis or PostgreSQL, with fields like session_id, user_id, created_at, last_activity, and status.
  • Session ID: generate secure, random IDs (e.g. UUIDs) on the server.
  • Link to LangGraph: use the session ID as the LangGraph thread_id, so memory and checkpoints are tied to the session.
  • Multi-device: for logged-in users, sessions are linked to the user ID instead of the device, so any device can load them.
  • Timeout and cleanup: use an expiry time (e.g. a TTL in Redis) or a scheduled cleanup job.
  • Monitoring: expose the number of active sessions through the existing health monitoring endpoints.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• User authentication, to link sessions to users across devices.
  • A shared session store.
  • Coordination with the frontend, to store and send the session ID.

items.title: Risks
items.text:
• Session hijacking: if a session ID is exposed, someone else could access the conversation.
  • Wrong timeout: too short annoys users; too long wastes resources.
  • Sync conflicts: sending messages from two devices at the same time may cause ordering issues.
  • Guest users: guests cannot be synced across devices without an account.

items.title: In Scope
items.text:
• Session IDs and tracking.
  • Session timeout and cleanup.
  • Session resume on the same device.
  • Basic active session count in health monitoring.

items.title: Out of Scope (for now)
items.text:
• Multi-device synchronization.
  • Multiple conversations per user.
  • A detailed monitoring dashboard.

items.title: 7. Open Questions
items.text:
• What is the right inactivity timeout (e.g. 30 minutes, 1 hour, 24 hours)?
  • Should guest sessions be kept, and for how long?
  • Should a user have one ongoing conversation, or multiple conversations they can choose from?

items.title: 8. Business Impact
items.text:
• Lower server costs: closing inactive sessions saves server resources, so costs do not grow without need.
  • Fewer lost customers: users do not have to start over every time, so they are more likely to continue and buy.
  • Foundation for sales features: Conversation Memory Management and personal recommendations cannot work without sessions.
  • Better planning for the team: knowing the number of active sessions helps the team know when the system needs to scale.

items.title: Example
items.text: If 1,000 users open the chat and leave it, without session timeout the server keeps all 1,000 sessions open without need. With session timeout, they are closed automatically, and costs go down.

items.title: Testing & Quality Assurance
items.text: Priority: Low

items.title: The problem
items.text: Every time the team changes the agent, such as changing the prompt or adding a tool, there is no quick way to make sure the change did not break something that was working. So problems reach users first.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
• A/B testing framework: test two versions of the agent on different users, and see which one is better.
  • Automated conversation testing: ready test conversations run automatically on the agent.
  • Response quality validation: make sure answers are correct and suitable.
  • Regression testing suite: make sure old features still work after any change.

items.title: Example
items.text: The team changes the prompt to make answers shorter. Before the change goes live, 100 test conversations run automatically, and the results show that the agent forgot to mention the product price in 20 of them. So the team fixes the problem before users see it.

items.title: Functional Requirements
items.text:
• FR-01: A/B testing: the system can split users between two versions of the agent and compare the results.
  • FR-02: Automated testing: the system runs ready test conversations on the agent.
  • FR-03: Response quality: the system checks that answers include the required information and contain no errors.
  • FR-04: Regression testing: tests run before any change goes live.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
• Speed: tests finish in a reasonable time, so they do not delay changes.
  • Repeatability: the same test gives the same result every time, as much as possible.
  • Easy to extend: the team can add new tests easily.

items.title: 3. Data Requirements
items.text:
• Test conversation set: real customer questions in Arabic and English, covering all request types (product search, routine, orders, shipping), including hard cases such as unclear messages.
  • Expected answers: for each test question, what must be in the answer, such as the product name and price, and what must not be in it.
  • Quality criteria: clear rules for a good answer, such as length, style, and no wrong information. These are connected to Response Quality Improvements.
  • A/B testing data: the results of each version, such as purchase rate and ratings from Feedback Collection, to compare them.
  • Test environment: a copy of the tools and data separated from the real website, so tests do not create real orders.

items.title: 4. Assessment
items.text:
In my view, this feature is important for the team, especially regression testing:

  • Every change in the prompt can break something without anyone noticing.
  • The effort is medium, and we can start with a small test set.
  • A/B testing can wait, because it needs many users for the results to be clear.

items.title: User Engagement Features
items.text: Priority: Low

items.title: The problem
items.text: Users sometimes receive useful answers from the agent, such as a skincare routine or a product comparison, but they cannot easily save, find, or share them later. Once the conversation moves on, useful information gets lost.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
The feature lets users keep and reuse their conversations:

  • Conversation bookmarking: save a whole conversation to find it later.
  • Message starring and saving: save a specific answer, such as a routine or a product list.
  • Conversation export: download a conversation as PDF or JSON.
  • Share conversation snippets: share part of a conversation with others, such as a friend.
  • Conversation search: search through past conversations.

items.title: Example
items.text:
The agent builds a full morning and night skincare routine for a user. She stars the answer, so she can open it again next week without asking again.

Later, she searches her history for "sunscreen" and finds the conversation where the agent compared three sunscreens.

items.title: 2. Why It Matters
items.text:
• Saves time: users do not need to ask the same question again.
  • Useful long-term: routines and comparisons can be reused.
  • Sharing: users can share recommendations with friends, which may bring new customers.
  • More engagement: users return to the agent more often.

items.title: Functional Requirements
items.text:
• FR-01: Conversation bookmarking: users can bookmark conversations.
  • FR-02: Message starring: users can star and save individual messages.
  • FR-03: Conversation export: users can export conversations as PDF or JSON.
  • FR-04: Share snippets: users can share selected messages through a link.
  • FR-05: Conversation search: users can search their past conversations by keyword.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
• Privacy: shared snippets must not include personal information unless the user chooses it.
  • Security: users can only access, search, and export their own conversations.
  • Performance: search must return results quickly.
  • Language support: search works in Arabic and English.

items.title: 4. Technical Approach
items.text:
• Conversation storage: relies on stored conversations from Conversation Memory Management.
  • Bookmarks and stars: simple tables linking user_id to conversation_id or message_id.
  • Export: generate PDF and JSON files on the server from the stored conversation.
  • Sharing: create a shareable link with a read-only copy of the selected messages.
  • Search: keyword search over stored conversations, with possible semantic search later using the existing vector database.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Conversation Memory Management, for stored conversations.
  • User Profiles & Authentication, since these features need a logged-in user.
  • Frontend support for bookmark, star, export, and share actions.

items.title: Risks
items.text:
• Low usage: users may not use these features much, which is why the priority is low.
  • Privacy in sharing: shared conversations may contain personal details.
  • Storage growth: saving and exporting many conversations increases storage.

items.title: In Scope
items.text:
• Message starring and a "saved messages" list.
  • Conversation search by keyword.

items.title: Out of Scope (for now)
items.text:
• Conversation export to PDF and JSON.
  • Sharing snippets through links.
  • Semantic search.

items.title: 7. Open Questions
items.text:
• Do users currently have a conversation history screen in the chat?
  • Should shared snippets be public links, or only visible to logged-in users?
  • How long should saved conversations be kept?

items.title: User Preferences & Settings
items.text: Priority: Low

items.title: The problem
items.text: Every user has different preferences: some prefer Arabic, some English; some like a formal tone, others a casual one; some only buy certain brands or within a certain budget. Today, the agent does not store these preferences, so users must repeat them, and the agent cannot adapt its answers.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
The feature stores and uses each user's preferences:

  • Language preference: Arabic or English.
  • Notification preferences: which alerts the user wants, such as price alerts.
  • Communication style: formal or casual.
  • Product category interests: such as skin care, hair care, or perfumes.
  • Price range preferences: the user's usual budget.
  • Brand preferences: brands the user likes, or wants to avoid.

items.title: Example
items.text:
A user tells the agent once: "I prefer to talk in Arabic, keep it casual, and my budget is under 150 SAR."

In every future conversation, the agent answers in Arabic, uses a friendly tone, and recommends products under 150 SAR first.

items.title: 2. Why It Matters
items.text:
• Less repetition: users do not have to repeat their preferences.
  • More relevant results: products match the user's budget, brands, and interests.
  • Better experience: the agent talks in the user's preferred language and style.
  • Fewer unwanted notifications: users only receive the alerts they chose.

items.title: Functional Requirements
items.text:
• FR-01: Language preference storage: the agent saves and uses the user's preferred language.
  • FR-02: Notification preferences: users choose which notifications they receive.
  • FR-03: Communication style preference: the agent adapts between formal and casual tones.
  • FR-04: Product category interests: the agent saves categories the user is interested in and prioritizes them.
  • FR-05: Price range preferences: the agent saves the user's budget and uses it to filter or rank products.
  • FR-06: Brand preferences: the agent saves preferred and avoided brands.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
• User control: users can view, change, or reset their preferences at any time.
  • Privacy: preferences are stored securely and only used for this user.
  • Performance: loading preferences must not slow down responses.

items.title: 4. Technical Approach
items.text:
• Preferences store: a preferences table or document linked to the user ID, with fields such as language, tone, categories, price_min, price_max, preferred_brands, avoided_brands, and notifications.
  • Two ways to set preferences:
  • Explicitly, through a settings page or by asking the agent ("speak to me in Arabic").
  • Implicitly, by detecting preferences from conversations, then confirming them with the user before saving.
  • Using preferences: preferences are loaded at the start of each conversation and added to the agent's state. Language and tone are applied in the system prompt, while categories, price range, and brands are passed to the marketplace tools as filters.
  • Link to long-term memory: preferences can be stored as part of the long-term memory from Conversation Memory Management.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• User Profiles & Authentication, to link preferences to a user.
  • Conversation Memory Management, for long-term storage.
  • Marketplace tools that support filtering by price, brand, and category.

items.title: Risks
items.text:
• Wrong detected preferences: the agent may guess a preference incorrectly and keep using it.
  • Too narrow results: strict filters may hide good products the user would like.
  • Outdated preferences: users' budgets and interests change over time.

items.title: In Scope
items.text:
• Language preference.
  • Price range and brand preferences, set explicitly by the user.
  • Using these preferences in product search and ranking.

items.title: Out of Scope (for now)
items.text:
• Automatic detection of preferences from conversations.
  • Notification preferences.
  • Communication style preferences.
  • A full preferences settings page.

items.title: 7. Assessment
items.text: This feature is not important at the moment. Most GoCare customers are Saudi and talk in the Saudi dialect, so there is no real need to store language or communication style preferences for each user.

items.title: User Profiles & Authentication
items.text: Priority: Low

items.title: The problem
items.text: The agent currently protects its API with an API key, but it does not clearly know who the user is. Without a reliable user identity, the agent cannot save memory, preferences, or sessions for each user, and cannot treat logged-in users and guests differently.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
The feature gives the agent a clear and secure user identity:

  • Supports user registration and login, or connects to GoCare's existing accounts.
  • Manages user profiles, including preferences and settings.
  • Identifies the same user across different sessions.
  • Handles anonymous (guest) users and authenticated (logged-in) users differently.
  • Encrypts sensitive profile data.

items.title: Example
items.text:
A guest opens the chat and asks about sunscreens. The agent answers normally, but does not save long-term preferences.

Later, she logs in. The agent now recognizes her, links the conversation to her profile, and can remember her skin type in future conversations.

items.title: 2. Why It Matters
items.text:
• Foundation for personalization: memory, preferences, and personalized responses all need a reliable user identity.
  • Security: users can only access their own data, sessions, and carts.
  • Better experience for logged-in users: saved preferences and history across devices.
  • Privacy: sensitive profile data is protected.

items.title: Functional Requirements
items.text:
• FR-01: Registration and login: users can register and log in, or the agent uses GoCare's existing login.
  • FR-02: Profile management: users have a profile that stores their preferences and settings.
  • FR-03: User identification across sessions: the same user is recognized in every session and on every device.
  • FR-04: Anonymous vs authenticated handling: guests can chat with limited features, while logged-in users get full features such as memory and saved preferences.
  • FR-05: Profile data encryption: sensitive profile data is encrypted.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
• Security: authentication must use secure, standard methods, and tokens must be validated on every request.
  • Privacy: profile data must follow data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.
  • Performance: checking the user identity must not slow down responses.
  • Compatibility: must work with GoCare's existing user accounts, instead of creating a separate login.

items.title: 4. Technical Approach
items.text:
• Reuse GoCare's authentication: instead of building a new login system, the agent validates the token issued by GoCare's backend (e.g. a JWT) and reads the user ID from it.
  • User ID as the key: the authenticated user ID is used to link sessions, memory, preferences, and carts.
  • Guest users: generate a temporary guest ID stored on the device, with limited features and a short data retention period.
  • Guest to user: when a guest logs in, the current conversation can be linked to the user's account.
  • Profile store: store agent-specific profile data (e.g. language, communication style) in a profile table linked to the user ID.
  • Encryption: encrypt sensitive fields at rest, and use HTTPS for all communication.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• GoCare's existing user accounts and authentication service.
  • Coordination with the Backend and Frontend teams to pass the user token to the agent.

items.title: Risks
items.text:
• Identity spoofing: if the agent trusts a user ID sent in the request instead of a validated token, users could access other users' data.
  • Duplicate identities: the same person may appear as a guest and a logged-in user.
  • Two login systems: building a separate login for the agent would confuse users.

items.title: In Scope
items.text:
• Validating GoCare's user token and extracting the user ID.
  • Linking sessions and conversations to the user ID.
  • Basic guest handling with limited features.

items.title: Out of Scope (for now)
items.text:
• A separate registration and login system for the agent.
  • Linking guest conversations to accounts after login.
  • Full profile management screens.

items.title: 7. Open Questions
items.text:
• Does GoCare's backend issue tokens (e.g. JWT) that the agent can validate?
  • Which features should guests have?
  • Which profile fields are considered sensitive and need encryption?

items.title: 8. Assessment
items.text: This feature is not very important at the moment. It is not important for the agent to know or say the user's name. What matters more is that the agent helps the user find what she wants.

items.title: Example
items.text: A user asks for a moisturizer for oily skin. It does not matter much if the agent says "Hello Sara". What matters is that it recommends the right moisturizer.

items.title: Voice Interface
items.text: Priority: Low

items.title: The problem
items.text: Some users prefer to speak instead of typing, especially on mobile. Many users in Saudi Arabia send voice notes on WhatsApp. The agent currently understands only written text.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
• Speech-to-text for voice queries: the user speaks, and the agent understands.
  • Text-to-speech responses: the agent answers with voice.
  • WhatsApp voice message support: the agent understands voice notes sent on WhatsApp.
  • Voice command shortcuts: such as "Where is my order?" by voice.

items.title: Example
items.text: A user sends a voice note on WhatsApp: "I have dry skin and I want a good moisturizer." The agent converts the voice to text and answers her with recommendations.

items.title: Functional Requirements
items.text:
• FR-01: Speech-to-text: the agent converts voice messages into text.
  • FR-02: Text-to-speech: the agent can answer with a voice message.
  • FR-03: WhatsApp voice notes: the agent understands voice notes from WhatsApp.
  • FR-04: Voice commands: the agent understands short voice commands.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
• Dialect accuracy: speech-to-text must understand the Saudi dialect well.
  • Speed: voice conversion must not delay the answer much.
  • Privacy: voice recordings are stored securely, or deleted after conversion.

items.title: 3. Data Requirements
items.text:
• Speech-to-text service: a service that supports Arabic and the Saudi dialect, such as Whisper or a cloud service, with its cost per minute.
  • Saudi voice samples: real recordings of customer questions in the Saudi dialect, to test conversion accuracy before launching the feature.
  • Product and brand names: a list of brand and product names, because they are often foreign, and the voice service may understand them incorrectly.
  • Text-to-speech service: if the agent answers with voice, a natural Arabic voice that fits GoCare's style is needed.
  • Recording storage rules: how long recordings are kept, or whether they are deleted right after conversion.

items.title: 4. Assessment
items.text:
In my view, this feature is not important at the moment:

  • The effort is very high.
  • It needs Multi-Channel Support (WhatsApp) to be built first.
  • The Saudi dialect and brand names make conversion accuracy harder.
  • Later, we can start with a small part only: understanding WhatsApp voice notes.

items.title: Recommendation System
items.text:
Short-term roadmap goals for the GoCare recommendation system.

Feature Priority (Original Roadmap) Importance After the Meeting (%) Smart Salon Services High 60% Skincare Routine Advisor High 50% Personalized Marketing High 80% Churn Prediction High 100% Visual Search High 80% Model Compression Medium 60% Analytics Dashboard High 30% Demand Forecasting High 40% Automated Content Tagging Moderate 90% Sentiment Analysis Moderate 50%

items.title: The problem
items.text:
As GoCare's AI systems grow, three challenges appear:

  • Models are trained once and do not improve by themselves from user reactions.
  • Neither users nor the team know why a product was recommended.
  • Choosing and tuning models takes a lot of manual effort from the team.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
AI/ML Innovation introduces three advanced approaches:

  • Reinforcement Learning (RL) for dynamic optimization: a model that learns by trying. It recommends something, observes whether the user clicks or buys, and improves itself over time.
  • Explainable AI (XAI): the system explains why it made a recommendation or prediction.
  • AutoML integration: tools that automatically try many models and settings, and choose the best one.

Example:

Approach Example Reinforcement Learning The homepage tries different product orders, learns which order leads to more purchases, and keeps improving it Explainable AI "Recommended because you bought a cleanser for oily skin" AutoML Instead of the team manually testing 10 models for Demand Forecasting, AutoML tests them and picks the best

In short, these approaches make the AI systems self-improving, understandable, and easier to build.

items.title: 2. Current System Status
items.text:
Based on the information available in this report:

  • GoCare has a recommendation system and plans several AI features, such as Demand Forecasting, Churn Prediction, and Collaborative Filtering.
  • The current models are trained and tuned manually.
  • It is not yet confirmed whether recommendation results are explained to users.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • These approaches build on the other AI features, so they come after them.
  • They improve how all models are built, measured, and explained.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to make GoCare's AI systems continuously improve, more trustworthy, and faster to develop.

Expected benefits:

  • Continuous improvement: recommendations and placements improve automatically from user feedback.
  • More trust: users and the team understand why the system makes each decision.
  • Faster development: less manual work to choose and tune models.
  • Easier debugging: explanations help the team find and fix wrong results.

Example:

If Churn Prediction marks a customer as high-risk, Explainable AI shows the reasons, such as "no purchase in 90 days" and "fewer visits", so the marketing team knows how to act.

Priority: Long-term vision, according to the roadmap.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Team Lead
items.text:
1. Which approach should come first?

Explainable AI, AutoML, or Reinforcement Learning?

2. Where should explanations appear?

To users on the website, to the internal team only, or both?

3. Which problems should Reinforcement Learning optimize?

For example, the order of recommendations, discount levels, or notification timing?

4. Is there a budget for AutoML tools or cloud services?

items.title: 4.2 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Is user feedback (clicks, purchases) logged quickly enough to train Reinforcement Learning models?
  2. Is there an A/B testing setup that can safely test new strategies?
  3. Which models are currently in production, and how are they trained and deployed?
  4. Is there a model monitoring setup?

items.title: 4.3 Shared Question
items.text:
How do we safely test self-learning systems?

The team lead agrees on safety limits, and the technical team confirms how to test and monitor them.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Reinforcement Learning optimization

The system must learn from user feedback to improve a chosen decision, such as the order of recommendations.

FR-02: Explanations for recommendations

The system must provide a simple reason for each recommendation.

FR-03: Explanations for predictions

Prediction models, such as Churn Prediction, must show the main factors behind each result.

FR-04: AutoML model selection

The team must be able to use AutoML to automatically compare and select models for a given problem.

Proposed additional requirements (need confirmation):

  • FR-05: Showing explanations to users on the website.
  • FR-06: Safety limits for Reinforcement Learning, such as maximum discount.
  • FR-07: Dashboards for model explanations and performance.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Safety

Self-learning systems must work within clear limits and be easy to stop.

2. Transparency

Explanations must be simple and correct.

3. Reliability

If an advanced model fails, the system must fall back to a simpler model.

4. Monitoring

Model performance must be monitored continuously.

5. Cost

Tools and compute resources must be justified by the improvement in results.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text: Data Purpose Status User Feedback (clicks, purchases) Train Reinforcement Learning Partly available; real-time logging unconfirmed Model Inputs & Outputs Generate explanations Depends on each model Training Datasets AutoML experiments Depends on each feature A/B Testing Results Safely test new strategies Not collected yet

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
• Explainable AI: standard methods, such as SHAP, can explain many models. Simple rule-based explanations can also be used for recommendations.
  • AutoML: many tools and cloud services exist for automatic model selection and tuning.
  • Reinforcement Learning: simple forms, such as multi-armed bandits, are practical for testing and optimizing recommendation orders. Full Reinforcement Learning is more complex and risky.

Initial assessment: Explainable AI and AutoML are technically feasible and relatively low-risk. Reinforcement Learning is feasible in simple forms, but needs careful testing and safety limits.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Models from other features, such as Collaborative Filtering, Demand Forecasting, and Churn Prediction, once they are built.
  • The Analytics Dashboard and A/B testing setup.
  • Model monitoring and deployment processes.
  • Collaboration between the Data, Backend, and Recommendation teams.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Unsafe learning

Reinforcement Learning may learn strategies that increase clicks but hurt long-term trust or profit.

2. Misleading explanations

Simplified explanations may not fully reflect how the model works.

3. Over-reliance on AutoML

AutoML may choose models that are hard to understand or maintain.

4. Complexity and cost

These approaches add complexity to the system.

Example:

If a Reinforcement Learning model learns that showing only discounted products increases clicks, it may reduce profit, which is why it must be limited and monitored.

items.title: Assessment
items.text:
Overall: not a priority for now

In my view, this feature should be postponed as a whole. However, each part is different in effort and value:

Part Effort Importance now Explainable AI (simple version) Very easy Medium, worth doing AutoML Easy Low Reinforcement Learning Hard Very low

1. Explainable AI (simple version): easy and worth doing

The simple version does not need AI. When a product is recommended because of another product the customer bought, we show the reason next to it, such as: "Recommended because you bought a cleanser for oily skin." This should take about one or two days, if the recommendation system already knows why each product was recommended. It also helps customers trust the recommendations more.

2. AutoML: easy, but not needed now

Ready-made libraries can do this with a few lines of code. However, it is useful only when there are many models and a lot of data. Since most models were postponed because data is still limited, it would not make a real difference now.

3. Reinforcement Learning: hard, and not the right time

  • It needs a very large number of visitors for the model to learn quickly.
  • It needs an A/B testing and monitoring setup.
  • It carries a risk: the model may learn the wrong behavior, such as showing only discounted products because they get more clicks, which reduces profit.

Suggestion: postpone the feature, and start only with the simple version of Explainable AI, since it is easy and gives value quickly.

items.title: 1. Feature Overview
items.text:
Analytics Dashboard is an internal dashboard that shows how well GoCare's recommendation system is performing, and how users interact with the website.

The dashboard covers four main areas:

  • Recommendation CTR: how often users click on recommendations compared to how often they are shown.
  • Popular products tracking: the most viewed, added to cart, and purchased products.
  • User engagement metrics: visits, active users, session duration, and pages viewed.
  • Conversion rates: how many recommendation clicks lead to actual purchases or bookings.

Example:

The team opens the dashboard and sees that recommendations on product pages have a 12% CTR, while recommendations on the homepage have only 4%, which helps them decide where to improve.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare shows recommendations to users, but it is not yet confirmed whether recommendation views and clicks are tracked.
  • It is not yet confirmed which analytics tools are used today (e.g. Google Analytics or an internal tool).
  • The other features in this roadmap all define success metrics, but there is no central place to view them yet.
  • GoCare already has an Admin Dashboard that shows information about customers, and it is used by more than one admin.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • Tracking must be confirmed or added before the dashboard can show reliable numbers.
  • The dashboard can become the place where all features' success metrics are measured.
  • The new analytics can be added to the existing Admin Dashboard, instead of building a separate dashboard.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to measure the real impact of the recommendation system and support data-driven decisions.

Expected benefits:

  • Clear visibility of whether recommendations increase sales.
  • Faster detection of problems, such as a sudden drop in clicks.
  • Better decisions on which features and placements to invest in.
  • One shared view of performance for management and the technical team.

Example:

After launching Smart Salon Services, management can see in the dashboard how many bookings came from recommendations, instead of guessing.

Priority: High, according to the roadmap.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Are recommendation impressions and clicks currently tracked?
  2. Can purchases and bookings be linked back to the recommendation that led to them?
  3. Which analytics tools or databases are already in use?
  4. What tool or framework is the existing Admin Dashboard built with, and can new charts be added to it?
  5. How long is event data stored?

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Recommendation CTR

The dashboard must show recommendation clicks divided by impressions, by placement (e.g. homepage, product page, cart).

FR-02: Popular products tracking

The dashboard must show the most viewed, added to cart, and purchased products.

FR-03: User engagement metrics

The dashboard must show visits, active users, session duration, and pages per session.

FR-04: Conversion rates

The dashboard must show how many recommendation clicks lead to purchases or bookings.

FR-05: Filtering

Users must be able to filter metrics by date range, placement, and product category.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-06: Scheduled reports by email.
  • FR-07: Alerts when a key metric drops suddenly.
  • FR-08: A/B test results for features such as Personalized Marketing.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Accuracy

The numbers must be correct and consistent with other company reports.

2. Performance

The dashboard must load quickly, even for long date ranges.

3. Access Control

Only authorized admins can access the analytics. Since more than one admin uses the Admin Dashboard, access can be controlled by role, so each admin sees only the metrics relevant to their work.

4. Privacy & Security

The dashboard must show aggregated numbers, not personal customer data, in line with data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.

5. Reliability

Tracking must not slow down the website for users.

Note: target values for data freshness and loading time must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Recommendation Impressions Calculate CTR Unconfirmed Recommendation Clicks Calculate CTR and conversion Unconfirmed Product Views Track popular products Unconfirmed Add-to-Cart Events Track popular products and funnel Unconfirmed Purchases & Bookings Calculate conversion rates Purchases available in the recommendation system; bookings unconfirmed Sessions & Visits Measure user engagement Unconfirmed

Example:

If recommendation impressions are not tracked, CTR cannot be calculated, even if clicks are recorded.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version starts with:

  • Tracking: record recommendation impressions, clicks, and conversions as events.

Later, improvements can be added, such as automatic alerts and A/B test reporting.

Initial assessment: technically feasible. The main effort is in adding reliable tracking; building the dashboard itself is relatively simple once the data exists.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Event tracking on the website for recommendations, views, carts, and purchases.
  • A database or analytics store for the events.
  • Collaboration between the Frontend, Backend, Data, and Recommendation teams.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Missing tracking

If events are not tracked today, there will be no historical data at launch.

2. Inconsistent definitions

Different teams may calculate metrics such as conversion differently.

3. Data volume

Tracking every impression can create large amounts of data.

Example:

If tracking is added today, the dashboard will only show data from today onwards, so it cannot compare with previous months.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. The feature is important

The Analytics Dashboard is considered useful and important, since it helps the team measure the impact of the other features.

2. Not a top priority right now

The feature is not a top priority at the moment. It stays in the plan, and work on it will start after the more urgent features.

3. Built inside the existing Admin Dashboard

The analytics will be added to GoCare's existing Admin Dashboard, which is used by more than one admin, instead of building a separate dashboard.

4. Used by the Admin Dashboard admins

The analytics are used by the admins who already use the Admin Dashboard.

5. Recommendation metrics are the most important

The most important numbers are the recommendation metrics, such as how often recommendations are clicked and how many lead to purchases.

6. How a conversion from a recommendation is counted

A purchase is counted as a conversion from a recommendation when the customer buys the product through the recommendation.

مثال:

سيعمل الفريق أولًا على الميزات الأكثر إلحاحًا.

  • بعد ذلك: تُضاف الأرقام الجديدة إلى لوحة التحكم التي يستخدمها المسؤولون حاليًا.
  • النتيجة: يرى المسؤولون في مكان واحد كم زادت المبيعات والحجوزات بفضل كل ميزة.

items.title: 1. Feature Overview
items.text:
Automated Content Tagging aims to automatically classify GoCare products and add the right attributes and categories to them, by reading product names and descriptions in Arabic and English, instead of entering this information manually for each product.

The feature has three main parts:

  • Category classification: assigning each product to the correct category and sub-category (e.g. skin care, then cleanser).
  • Attribute extraction: extracting product attributes from the text, such as suitable skin or hair type, key ingredients, scent, shade, size, and gender.
  • Bilingual support: handling product content written in Arabic, English, or a mix of both.

Example:

For a product named "Niacinamide Gel Cleanser for Oily Skin", the system extracts: category = skin care, product type = cleanser, skin type = oily, key ingredient = niacinamide.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare offers products across many categories, such as skin care, hair care, makeup, perfumes, personal care, men's care, and beauty devices.
  • The website supports both Arabic and English.
  • GoCare hosts products from different brands and sellers, so product names and descriptions may be written in different styles and languages.
  • Products are already tagged with their type or routine step (e.g. cleanser, serum, shampoo). It is not yet confirmed whether they have other structured attributes, such as skin type and ingredients.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • Product text already exists and can be used as input for the model.
  • Inconsistent product descriptions make manual tagging slow, which is the main reason for this feature.
  • Several other roadmap features depend on good product attributes, so this feature can support them.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to make product data complete and consistent, which improves search, filtering, and recommendations, while reducing manual work.

Expected benefits:

  • Less manual effort when adding new products.
  • More consistent categories and attributes across all sellers and brands.
  • Better search and filters, such as filtering by skin type or ingredient.
  • Better recommendations, since recommendation features rely on product attributes.

Example:

The Skincare Routine Advisor needs each product to be tagged with skin type and ingredients. Products already have their routine step, so automated tagging can add the missing attributes to thousands of products instead of doing it manually.

Business Impact: Moderate, according to the client's assessment.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. How many products are in the catalog, and how many already have categories and attributes?
  2. Are product names and descriptions stored in both Arabic and English, or in one language only?
  3. Is there a database structure ready to store new attributes, such as skin type and ingredients?
  4. Are there already correctly tagged products that can be used to train or test the model?
  5. Is there an existing API for adding or updating product attributes?

items.title: 4.2 Shared Question for the Client and Data Team
items.text:
What is the official list of tags?

The client defines which categories and attributes should exist and what their allowed values are, and the data team confirms how they will be stored and used by search and recommendations.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Category classification

The system must assign each product to the correct category and sub-category.

Example: a product named "Argan Oil Hair Mask" is classified as hair care, then hair mask.

FR-02: Attribute extraction

The system must extract product attributes from the product name and description.

Example: "Fragrance-free moisturizer for sensitive skin" gives skin type = sensitive and fragrance = free.

FR-03: Arabic and English support

The system must handle product text in Arabic, English, or a mix of both.

Example: the Arabic and English descriptions of the same product give the same tags.

FR-04: Confidence score

The system must give a confidence score for each tag, so low-confidence tags can be reviewed.

Example: skin type = oily (95% confidence) is applied directly, while scent = floral (55% confidence) is sent for review.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-05: A review screen where the team can approve or correct suggested tags.
  • FR-06: Suggesting tags to sellers while they add a new product.
  • FR-07: Bulk tagging of the existing catalog.
  • FR-08: Learning from manual corrections to improve future tags.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Accuracy

Tags must be accurate enough to be used in search, filters, and recommendations, and their accuracy must be measured on a test set.

2. Consistency

The same type of product must always get the same tags, regardless of language or writing style.

3. Performance

Tagging a single product must be fast enough to work while a product is being added, and bulk tagging must be able to process the full catalog.

4. Reviewability

Every automatic tag must be traceable, so the team knows whether it was added by the model or by a person.

5. Reliability

A failure in the tagging service must not prevent products from being added or shown on the website.

Note: target values for tagging accuracy and processing time must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Product Names & Descriptions Main input for tagging Exists on the website Arabic and English Content Bilingual tagging Exists on the website; completeness unconfirmed Current Categories Category classification Exists on the website Official Attribute List Define which tags to extract Not available; needs to be agreed Correctly Tagged Products Train and test the model Unconfirmed Product Images (optional) Support tagging when text is missing Exists on the website

Example:

If product descriptions are very short, such as "Cream 50 ml", the model cannot reliably tell the skin type or ingredients, so these products may need manual review or images as extra input.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can be built with a combination of simple rules and Natural Language Processing:

  • Keyword and rule-based extraction: detecting clear terms such as "oily skin", "بشرة دهنية", "niacinamide", or "shampoo".
  • Text classification models: classifying products into categories using a multilingual model that supports Arabic and English.
  • Large Language Models (LLMs): extracting structured attributes from product descriptions, with a fixed list of allowed values.

Later, improvements can be tested, such as:

  • Fine-tuning a model on GoCare's correctly tagged products.
  • Combining product text and images for better accuracy.

Initial assessment: technically feasible, especially with current multilingual models. The main effort is in agreeing on the official tag list and preparing a test set to measure accuracy.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• An agreed official list of categories and attributes.
  • Access to product names and descriptions.
  • A database structure to store the new attributes.
  • A set of correctly tagged products for testing.
  • Collaboration between the Data, Backend, and Recommendation teams, and the team that manages products.
  • Coordination with features that use product attributes, such as Skincare Routine Advisor and Visual Search.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Inconsistent product content

Sellers and brands write product descriptions in different styles, lengths, and languages.

2. Arabic language challenges

Arabic product text may include different spellings, dialect words, or a mix of Arabic and English.

3. Wrong tags

Wrong tags can lead to wrong filters and wrong recommendations, such as recommending a product for the wrong skin type.

4. Missing information

Some products may not mention important attributes at all in their text.

Example:

If a cleanser is wrongly tagged as suitable for dry skin, the Skincare Routine Advisor may recommend it to the wrong users, which is why low-confidence tags must be reviewed.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. The feature is important

Automated Content Tagging is considered an important feature for GoCare, since complete and correct product information improves search, filters, and recommendations, and reduces manual work.
