تمت إضافة منتج جديد إلى الموقع باسم: Niacinamide Gel Cleanser for Oily Skin. يقرأ النظام الاسم ويضيف معلومات المنتج بنفسه، دون أن يكتبها أحد يدويًا:

  • نوع المنتج: غسول
  • نوع البشرة: دهنية
  • المكوّن الأساسي: النياسيناميد

بعد ذلك، يمكن للعميلة أن تجد المنتج عندما تختار فلتر البشرة الدهنية، ويقترحه روتين العناية بالبشرة على العميلات ذوات البشرة الدهنية فقط.

items.title: 1. Feature Overview
items.text:
Churn Prediction aims to identify GoCare customers who are likely to stop buying or booking, before they actually leave, so the business can act early to keep them.

The feature has three main parts:

  • Identifying at-risk customers: a model that estimates, for each customer, the probability that they will stop using GoCare, based on their past behavior.
  • Proactive retention campaigns: sending targeted offers or reminders to at-risk customers before they leave.
  • Customer Lifetime Value (CLV): estimating how much each customer is expected to spend on GoCare over time, to understand the value of each customer.

Example:

A customer who used to buy skin care products every month has not purchased in three months. The system marks her as at-risk, and she receives a WhatsApp message with a personal discount code to encourage her to buy again.

Note: unlike the other features in this section, this is a prediction and analytics feature rather than a product recommendation feature, although it relies on the same customer data.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare combines a beauty products store with salon booking, so customer activity includes both purchases and bookings.
  • The website already offers loyalty incentives, such as 1,000 points on registration, which could be used in retention offers.
  • It is not yet confirmed how much purchase and booking history is stored, and for how long.
  • It is not yet confirmed whether customer activity, such as visits and logins, is recorded.
  • Customers already confirm their orders on WhatsApp.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • The prediction model depends on enough historical customer data, which must be confirmed first.
  • Existing loyalty points and offers can be reused in retention campaigns.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to reduce customer loss and increase revenue by keeping existing customers, which is usually cheaper than acquiring new ones.

Expected benefits:

  • Fewer customers leaving GoCare.
  • Retention efforts focused on customers who are actually at risk.
  • Acting early, before customers are lost completely.
  • A clearer understanding of why customers leave.

Example:

Instead of waiting until customers are lost, GoCare sends every customer who has not bought anything for three months a personal discount code on WhatsApp.

Business Impact: High, according to the client's assessment.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. How far back does purchase and booking history go?
  2. Is customer activity recorded (visits, logins, searches, cart activity)?
  3. Are order values stored, so customer spending can be calculated?
  4. Are returns, cancellations, and refunds recorded?
  5. Can prediction results be stored and shared with the WhatsApp messaging system?

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Churn risk scoring

The system must estimate a churn risk score for each customer.

Example: customer A has an 80% probability of churning, customer B has 10%.

FR-02: At-risk customer list

The system must produce a list of at-risk customers, updated regularly.

Example: a weekly list of customers with high churn risk.

FR-03: Customer Lifetime Value calculation

The system must estimate the expected lifetime value of each customer.

Example: customer A is expected to spend 3,000 SAR over the next year.

FR-04: Retention campaign support

The system must provide at-risk segments that can be used in retention campaigns.

Example: high-risk customers receive a WhatsApp message with a personal discount code, encouraging them to buy again from the website.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-05: A dashboard showing churn risk, CLV, and retention campaign results.
  • FR-06: Main reasons behind each customer's risk score (e.g. fewer visits, longer time since last purchase).
  • FR-07: Tracking whether retained customers actually returned after a campaign.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Model Accuracy

Predictions must be accurate enough to be useful, and measured before launch.

2. Explainability

The business team should be able to understand why a customer is marked as at-risk.

3. Regular Updates

Risk scores must be refreshed regularly as customer behavior changes.

4. Privacy & Security

Customer data must be protected and used in line with data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.

5. Reliability

A failure in the prediction pipeline must not affect the website or other systems.

Note: target values for model accuracy and update frequency must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Purchase History Track buying patterns and spending Available in the product recommendation system Booking History Track salon customer activity Unconfirmed Order Values Calculate spending and CLV Unconfirmed Customer Activity (visits, logins) Detect declining engagement Unconfirmed Cart Activity Detect abandoned purchases Unconfirmed Returns & Cancellations Detect dissatisfaction signals Unconfirmed Customer Profile Registration date and basic attributes Unconfirmed Campaign Results Measure retention success Not collected yet

Example:

If GoCare has only a few months of purchase history, the model will not have enough examples of customers who left, and its predictions will be unreliable.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can start simple:

  • Rule-based risk scoring: e.g. customers with no purchase in three months are marked as at-risk.
  • RFM analysis: scoring customers by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary value to identify valuable and at-risk customers.
  • Simple CLV estimate: average order value multiplied by purchase frequency and expected customer lifetime.

When enough history is available, Machine Learning models can be tested, such as:

  • Classification models (e.g. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) to predict churn probability.
  • Probabilistic CLV models to estimate future customer value more accurately.

Initial assessment: technically feasible, but the quality of predictions depends mainly on the amount and history of customer data available.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Enough historical purchase, booking, and activity data.
  • The agreed definition of churn: no purchase for three months.
  • The WhatsApp Business API, to send win-back messages.
  • Collaboration between the Data, Backend, and Recommendation teams, and the marketing team.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Limited history

If GoCare is relatively new, there may not be enough examples of churned customers to train a model.

2. Unclear churn definition

Customers buy beauty products at different frequencies, so one fixed definition may not fit all customers.

3. Acting too late or too often

Predictions are only useful if retention actions follow quickly, without overwhelming customers with offers.

4. Measuring real impact

Some at-risk customers may return on their own, so retention results must be compared with a control group.

Example:

If 30% of at-risk customers return after a campaign, but 25% of a similar group that received nothing also returned, the campaign's real impact is only 5%.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. Orders are confirmed on WhatsApp

Customers already confirm their orders on WhatsApp, similar to how shipping companies such as Bosta work. This existing WhatsApp channel will be reused.

2. Handoff to human support on WhatsApp

If a customer wants to make any change to their order, and the system cannot understand the request, the conversation is transferred to a human on a dedicated WhatsApp support number.

3. Win-back messages on WhatsApp

If a customer has not bought anything for three months, the system sends them a WhatsApp message with a discount code, encouraging them to buy again from the website. This replaces sending retention offers through the Personalized Marketing feature.

4. All inactive customers receive the code

Every customer who has not bought anything for three months receives the discount code. Customer Lifetime Value is not used to decide who receives the offer.

Requirements for this:

  • Messages must use WhatsApp message templates approved by Meta.
  • Messages are sent only to customers who agreed to receive marketing messages.
  • Each customer receives a personal discount code, so purchases from the message can be tracked.
  • Each inactive customer receives the message only once in a set period, since every WhatsApp marketing message has a cost.

مثال:

عميلتان في موقفين مختلفين على واتساب.

  • عميلة تريد تغيير عنوان طلبها على واتساب: لا يستطيع النظام فهم طلبها، فتُحوَّل إلى رقم الدعم على واتساب، ويساعدها أحد موظفي الدعم.
  • عميلة لم تشترِ أي شيء منذ ثلاثة أشهر: تصلها رسالة على واتساب فيها كود خصم شخصي ورابط للموقع، فتستخدم الكود وتشتري مرة أخرى.

Open question:

  • Discount value and validity: the discount value and how long the code stays valid are still to be agreed.

Blocker:

  • Is the WhatsApp Business API already connected to GoCare's system?

    To send messages automatically, without someone sending them manually, the WhatsApp Business API is required. If it is already used to confirm orders, the same connection can be reused. If not, it must be set up first, and the win-back messages cannot be sent until then.

items.title: The problem
items.text: Most simple recommendation systems recommend products that are similar to what the user viewed or bought, based on product attributes such as category or brand. This is called content-based filtering. It works, but it has a limit: it only recommends products similar to what the user already knows, and rarely helps them discover something new that they may like.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
Collaborative Filtering recommends products based on the behavior of similar users, not only on product attributes.

Example:

User Bought User A Cleanser, Toner, Moisturizer, Sunscreen, Vitamin C Serum User B Cleanser, Toner, Moisturizer, Sunscreen

User A and User B bought the same four products, so their tastes are similar. User A also bought a Vitamin C Serum, so the system recommends it to User B, even though it is not similar to anything User B has bought.

The roadmap describes two techniques:

  • User-to-user similarity: finding users with similar behavior and recommending what they liked.
  • Matrix factorization: a mathematical method that analyzes a large table of all users and all products, and discovers hidden patterns in their preferences.

items.title: What "hybrid" means
items.text:
The goal is a hybrid recommendation approach that combines:

  • Content-based filtering: "this product is similar to what you bought".
  • Collaborative filtering: "users similar to you bought this".

Combining both gives more accurate and more varied recommendations than either one alone.

items.title: 2. Current System Status
items.text:
Based on the information available in this report:

  • GoCare already has a product recommendation system in production.
  • It is not yet confirmed which methods the current system uses.
  • It is not yet confirmed how much user interaction data is recorded (views, clicks, add-to-cart, purchases, bookings).

What does this mean for the feature?

  • The new method must be added to the existing system, not built from scratch.
  • Collaborative filtering depends heavily on the amount of interaction data available.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to make recommendations more accurate and more varied, so users discover more products they like and buy more.

Expected benefits:

  • Better recommendations: based on real behavior, not only product attributes.
  • More discovery: users find products they would not have searched for.
  • Higher conversion and order value: more relevant products shown to each user.
  • Improves over time: recommendations get better as more users interact with the website.

Example:

A user who only buys skin care products may receive a recommendation for a hair care product that many similar users bought, which content-based filtering alone would not suggest.

Priority: High, according to the roadmap.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Team Lead / Client
items.text:
1. Where should the hybrid recommendations be used?

Homepage, product pages, cart, chatbot, or all of them?

2. How should the new recommendations be evaluated before launch?

Offline tests on historical data, A/B testing with real users, or both?

3. Should salons and services be included?

Products only, or also salon services and bookings?

items.title: 4.2 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Which recommendation methods does the current system use?
  2. Which user interactions are recorded (views, clicks, add-to-cart, purchases, bookings)?
  3. How many users and how many interactions are available?
  4. Are guest users tracked, or only logged-in users?
  5. How often is the current recommendation model retrained?

items.title: 4.3 Shared Question
items.text:
Is there enough interaction data?

Collaborative filtering needs many users interacting with many products. The data team confirms the amount of data, and the team lead decides whether to start now or after collecting more data.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: User-to-user similarity

The system must find users with similar behavior and use their interactions to recommend products.

FR-02: Matrix factorization model

The system must train a matrix factorization model on user-product interactions to predict which products each user may like.

FR-03: Hybrid recommendations

The system must combine collaborative filtering results with content-based results into one recommendation list.

Example: half of the recommendations come from similar products, and half from similar users, ranked together.

FR-04: Cold-start handling

The system must fall back to content-based or popular products for new users and new products with no interactions.

Example: a new user with no history sees popular products, then personalized recommendations after a few interactions.

Proposed additional requirements (need confirmation):

  • FR-05: Regular retraining of the model with new interaction data.
  • FR-06: A/B testing of hybrid recommendations against the current system.
  • FR-07: Including salon services in the recommendations.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Performance

Recommendations must be returned quickly, without slowing down the website.

2. Scalability

The model must handle growth in users, products, and interactions.

3. Recommendation Quality

The hybrid approach must perform better than the current system on agreed metrics, such as click-through and conversion rates.

4. Privacy

User interaction data must be used in line with data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.

5. Reliability

If the new model fails, the system must fall back to the current recommendations.

Note: target values for response time and quality improvement must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Purchase History Main signal of user preferences Available in the product recommendation system Views, Clicks, Add-to-Cart Extra signals of interest Unconfirmed Booking History Include salon services Unconfirmed Ratings Explicit user preferences Feature exists; amount unconfirmed Product Attributes Content-based part of the hybrid model Exists; completeness needs review User IDs (logged in and guests) Link interactions to users Unconfirmed

Example:

If most users bought only one product, there is not enough overlap between users to find similar ones, and collaborative filtering will not work well.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
Collaborative filtering is a well-known and widely used approach:

  • Matrix factorization methods, such as ALS, are available in standard libraries and work well with purchase and click data.
  • User-to-user similarity can be calculated with simple similarity measures, such as cosine similarity.
  • Hybrid ranking can combine the scores of content-based and collaborative models.

Initial assessment: technically feasible, and it builds on the existing recommendation system. The main condition is having enough interaction data.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Enough user interaction data.
  • Access to the current recommendation system and its data.
  • Good product attributes for the content-based part, supported by Automated Content Tagging.
  • The Analytics Dashboard, to measure the impact of the new recommendations.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Cold start

New users and new products have no interactions, so collaborative filtering cannot recommend them.

2. Sparse data

If users interact with very few products, it is hard to find similar users.

3. Popularity bias

The model may keep recommending the same popular products to everyone.

4. Compute cost

Training on large interaction data may need more computing resources.

Example:

A new product added today has no purchases, so collaborative filtering will never recommend it. This is why the content-based part of the hybrid approach is still needed.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. The feature is important

Collaborative Filtering is considered an important feature for GoCare, since it helps users discover new products based on what similar users bought.

2. Not for now

The feature will not be built at the moment. It can start later, when the number of users becomes very large, since this method needs many users interacting with many products to work well.

مثال:

لكي يقترح النظام سيروم فيتامين سي على عميلة، يجب أن يجد أولًا عملاء آخرين لديهم ذوق مشابه لذوقها واشتروا هذا السيروم.

  • عندما يكون عدد المستخدمين قليلًا: يصعب العثور على عملاء متشابهين، لذلك لن تكون الاقتراحات دقيقة.
  • عندما يصبح عدد المستخدمين كبيرًا جدًا: يستطيع النظام العثور على عملاء متشابهين بسهولة، وعندها تكون الميزة مفيدة.

items.title: The problem
items.text:
Every product, campaign, and page on GoCare needs written content. Today, this content is written manually by the team or by sellers. As a result:

  • Some products have very short or missing descriptions.
  • Product descriptions are written in different styles and quality levels.
  • Writing marketing content in Arabic and English for thousands of products takes a lot of time.
  • Pages are not always written in a way that helps them appear in search engines such as Google.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
Content Creation uses AI to generate content automatically. The roadmap describes three parts:

  • AI-generated product descriptions: writing a clear description for each product, in Arabic and English, based on its name, attributes, and images.
  • SEO-optimized marketing copy: writing product pages and marketing texts in a way that helps them rank higher in search engines.
  • Personalized content feeds: showing each user content that matches their interests, such as tips, articles, and products.

Example:

Case Before After Product description "Cream 50 ml" A full description explaining the product type, suitable skin type, key ingredients, and how to use it Search visibility Product page with a short title only A page with a clear title and description that matches what users search for on Google Homepage The same content for every user A user interested in hair care sees hair care tips and products first

In short, the feature turns limited product information into complete, consistent, and personalized content.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare offers many products from different brands and sellers.
  • The website supports Arabic and English.
  • Product descriptions vary in length, style, and quality.
  • The AI Agent team already has work related to content enhancement in the chatbot.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • There is a clear need for consistent, high-quality product content.
  • The existing content enhancement work in the AI Agent team may be reused, so the work must be aligned to avoid building the same thing twice.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to improve product content quality and visibility, which helps users make buying decisions and brings more visitors from search engines.

Expected benefits:

  • Complete product pages: every product has a clear and useful description.
  • More visitors from search engines: better SEO brings more free traffic.
  • Faster product onboarding: new products are ready to sell faster.
  • More engagement: personalized content keeps users interested.

Example:

A new product added by a seller without a description gets a complete Arabic and English description in minutes, instead of waiting for the team to write it.

Priority: Long-term vision, according to the roadmap.

items.title: 4. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Product description generation

The system must generate product descriptions in Arabic and English from product names, attributes, and images.

FR-02: SEO-optimized content

The system must generate titles and descriptions that include relevant search keywords.

FR-03: Personalized content feeds

The system must show each user content that matches their interests.

FR-04: Human review

Generated content must be reviewable and editable before it is published.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-05: Generating marketing copy for campaigns, connected to Personalized Marketing.
  • FR-06: Checking generated content against a list of forbidden claims.
  • FR-07: Measuring the impact of new content on visits and sales.

items.title: 5. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Accuracy

Generated content must not include wrong information about products.

2. Safety & Compliance

Content must avoid medical claims and follow advertising rules in Saudi Arabia.

3. Consistency

Content must follow GoCare's brand voice in both languages.

4. Language Quality

Arabic content must be natural and correct, not a literal translation from English.

5. Traceability

It must be clear which content was generated by AI and who approved it.

items.title: 6. Data Requirements
items.text: Data Purpose Status Product Names & Attributes Input for writing descriptions Exists; completeness needs review Product Images Extra input for descriptions Exists on the website Brand Style Guide Keep a consistent voice Unconfirmed Search Keywords SEO optimization Unconfirmed User Interests Personalized content feeds Partly available through recommendation data List of Forbidden Claims Avoid unsafe or misleading content Not available; needs to be prepared

items.title: 7. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are very capable of writing product descriptions and marketing texts in Arabic and English. The first version can:

  • Use an LLM with a fixed template and product attributes as input.
  • Apply a brand style guide and a list of forbidden claims.
  • Send generated content for human review before publishing.

Initial assessment: technically feasible with current models. The main effort is in quality control, brand voice, and avoiding wrong or unsafe claims.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Good product attributes, supported by Automated Content Tagging.
  • A brand style guide and content rules.
  • Alignment with the AI Agent team's content enhancement work.
  • A review process with the content or marketing team.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Wrong information

AI may invent product details that are not true.

2. Medical claims

Skin care content may include claims such as "treats acne", which may not be allowed.

3. Repetitive content

Generated texts may sound too similar, which can hurt SEO and user experience.

4. Arabic quality

Generated Arabic may sound unnatural without careful prompts and review.

Example:

If the AI writes "this cream treats eczema" for a normal moisturizer, it creates a false medical claim, which is why human review and a forbidden claims list are required.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. The feature already exists

The team already has an AI content creation feature for product descriptions.

2. Current problems

The existing feature has several problems:

  • Edits are rejected: if the team edits anything in the description generated by the AI, the system rejects the edit, so they cannot change the text.
  • Required information that is not needed: the system forces the team to fill in specific product information, such as the expiry date or the country of origin, before it generates a description.
  • Unimportant data: this information is not important to the team, and filling it in for every product takes extra time.

3. What the team needs

  • Editable descriptions: the team must be able to edit the AI-generated description freely, and the edits must be saved.
  • Only important fields: the system should provide fields only for the information that is important for the product, and the team fills in these fields only.
  • No forced fields: information that is not important should be optional, or removed, instead of being required.

مثال:

يريد الفريق إضافة كريم مرطب إلى الموقع.

  • اليوم: يجبرهم النظام أولًا على إدخال تاريخ انتهاء الصلاحية وبلد المنشأ. ثم إذا غيّروا جملة واحدة في الوصف الذي كتبه الذكاء الاصطناعي، يرفض النظام التغيير.
  • ما يريده الفريق: يملؤون الحقول المهمة فقط، مثل نوع المنتج ونوع البشرة والمكونات الأساسية. ثم يكتب الذكاء الاصطناعي الوصف، ويستطيعون تعديله بحرية وحفظه.

items.title: The problem
items.text: Current recommendations depend on who the user is, such as their preferences and history. They do not consider the user's current situation, such as the time of day, where they are, or the weather. But beauty and care needs change with these conditions.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
Context-Aware Recommendations adjust recommendations based on the user's current context. The roadmap describes three types:

  • Time-based: recommendations change with the time of day, day of the week, or season.
  • Location-based: recommendations change with the user's city or area.
  • Weather-aware: recommendations change with the current weather, such as heat, humidity, or dust.

Example:

Context Recommendation Morning Sunscreen and day moisturizer Evening Night cream and makeup remover User in Jeddah (humid) Light, oil-free products User in Riyadh (dry) Richer moisturizers Very hot day Sunscreen with higher protection and cooling products Dusty weather Deep cleansers

In short, the same user may see different recommendations depending on when and where they open GoCare.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare serves customers in Saudi Arabia, with free shipping on the first order in Riyadh.
  • Saudi cities have very different climates, such as humid coastal cities and dry inland cities.
  • It is not yet confirmed whether the user's city is stored or detected.
  • Smart Salon Services already plans to use the user's location.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • Location and climate differences in Saudi Arabia make this feature especially relevant.
  • The location handling planned for Smart Salon Services can be reused.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to make recommendations feel more timely and relevant, which increases clicks and purchases.

Expected benefits:

  • More relevant recommendations: matching the user's real needs at that moment.
  • Higher conversion: users are more likely to buy what fits their current situation.
  • Better seasonal and daily planning: connected to Demand Forecasting.

Example:

On a very hot summer day in Riyadh, the homepage highlights high-protection sunscreens and light moisturizers, instead of showing the same products as in winter.

Priority: Long-term vision, according to the roadmap.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Client
items.text:
1. Which context should come first?

Time, location, or weather?

2. Where should context-aware recommendations appear?

Homepage, product pages, notifications, or the chatbot?

3. How should the user's location be determined?

From the delivery address, a city selected by the user, or the device location with permission?

4. Which cities should be supported first?

items.title: 4.2 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Is the user's city or delivery address stored?
  2. Can the website use a weather data service?
  3. Are product attributes available to match products with conditions, such as "oil-free" or "high SPF"?
  4. Can the recommendation system accept context as an extra input?

items.title: 4.3 Shared Question for the Client and Data Team
items.text:
Which rules connect context to products?

For example, which products should be prioritized in humid weather or at night? The client agrees on the rules, and the data team confirms that the needed product attributes exist.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Time-based recommendations

The system must adjust recommendations based on the time of day and season.

FR-02: Location-based recommendations

The system must adjust recommendations based on the user's city or area.

FR-03: Weather-aware recommendations

The system must adjust recommendations based on current weather conditions in the user's city.

FR-04: Fallback

If context is not available, the system must show normal recommendations.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-05: Explaining the reason, such as "Recommended for today's hot weather".
  • FR-06: Context-aware notifications, such as a sunscreen reminder on very hot days.
  • FR-07: Using context in the chatbot.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Performance

Adding context must not slow down recommendations.

2. Privacy

Location must only be used with the user's permission, in line with data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.

3. Reliability

If the weather service fails, normal recommendations must still work.

4. Relevance

Context rules must be reviewed to make sure they make sense for users.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text: Data Purpose Status User City / Location Location-based recommendations Unconfirmed Weather Data Weather-aware recommendations Not available; needs an external service Time and Date Time-based recommendations Available Product Attributes Match products to conditions Exists; completeness needs review Context Rules Connect conditions to products Not available; needs to be agreed Interaction Data with Context Measure and improve results Not collected yet

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can be rule-based:

  • Simple rules connect time, city, and weather to product attributes.
  • A weather service provides current conditions for the user's city.
  • The recommendation system boosts products that match the current context.

Later, Machine Learning models can learn which products perform best in each context, using interaction data.

Initial assessment: technically feasible, especially with rule-based logic. It depends on good product attributes and a reliable weather data source.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Product attributes, supported by Automated Content Tagging.
  • User location handling, shared with Smart Salon Services.
  • A weather data service.
  • Collaboration between the Data, Backend, and Recommendation teams.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Location permission

Many users may not share their location.

2. Weak rules

Wrong or obvious rules may make recommendations feel repetitive.

3. External service cost and reliability

Weather services may have costs or downtime.

4. Measuring impact

It may be hard to prove that context improved results without careful testing.

Example:

If the system recommends heavy moisturizers to a user in a humid city only because it is winter, the recommendation will feel wrong, which is why location and weather must be combined with time.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text: The feature is not important at all at the moment.

items.title: Context Awareness
items.text: Priority: High · Effort: High

items.title: The problem
items.text: People do not talk in complete, separate sentences. They refer to things mentioned earlier, ask short follow-up questions, and change topics. Without context awareness, the agent cannot understand messages such as "the second one", "is it suitable for me?", or "add it to the cart".

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
The feature helps the agent understand a conversation as a whole:

  • Understands conversations across multiple turns.
  • Resolves references, such as "it", "this one", "the second one", and "that product".
  • Handles follow-up questions.
  • Tracks the current topic, and handles topic changes.
  • Keeps track of the conversation state (e.g. browsing, comparing, adding to cart, checkout).

items.title: Example
items.text:
User: Show me vitamin C serums.

Agent: (shows three products)

User: How much is the second one?

User: Is it suitable for oily skin?

User: Has my last order shipped yet?

User: OK, add the serum to my cart.

The agent must know that "the second one", "it", and "the serum" all refer to the same product, and that the question about the order was a temporary topic change.

items.title: 2. Why It Matters
items.text:
• Natural conversations: users can talk normally, without repeating product names.
  • Fewer mistakes: the agent acts on the right product.
  • Better shopping flow: browsing, comparing, and adding to cart happen smoothly in one conversation.
  • Required for complex features: such as building a skincare routine in the chat.

items.title: Functional Requirements
items.text:
• FR-01: Multi-turn understanding: the agent understands each message in the context of previous messages.
  • FR-02: Reference resolution: the agent links references (pronouns, "that product", "the second one") to the correct item.
  • FR-03: Follow-up question handling: the agent answers short follow-up questions about the current item or topic.
  • FR-04: Topic tracking and switching: the agent detects topic changes, and can return to the previous topic.
  • FR-05: Conversation state management: the agent tracks the current stage of the conversation, such as browsing, comparing, cart, or checkout.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
• Accuracy: references must be resolved correctly, especially before actions such as adding to cart.
  • Safety: when a reference is unclear, the agent must ask for clarification instead of guessing.
  • Performance: context handling must not noticeably slow down responses.
  • Language support: works in Arabic and English, including mixed messages.

items.title: 4. Technical Approach
items.text:
• Structured state in LangGraph: besides the message history, store structured context in the graph state, such as last_shown_products, current_product, current_topic, and conversation_stage.
  • Reference resolution: when the agent shows products, save them in order in the state. References like "the second one" are mapped to that list.
  • Query rewriting: before calling tools, the agent rewrites short follow-up messages into complete requests (e.g. "is it suitable for oily skin?" becomes "is Vitamin C Serum X suitable for oily skin?").
  • Topic tracking: save the current topic in the state, and keep the previous topic when the user temporarily switches.
  • Clarification: if a reference matches more than one item, the agent asks the user which one they mean.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Conversation Memory Management, to keep the conversation history and state.
  • Session Management, to keep the state tied to the right conversation.
  • Marketplace and cart tools that return product IDs, so references can be linked to real products.

items.title: Risks
items.text:
• Wrong references: the agent may add the wrong product to the cart.
  • Ambiguity: messages like "this one" may be unclear when several products were discussed.
  • Arabic references: Arabic pronouns and dialect expressions (e.g. "ده", "اللي قبله") make resolution harder.
  • Higher costs: query rewriting adds extra model calls.

items.title: 7. Open Questions
items.text:
• Should the agent always confirm before actions like adding to cart, or only when the reference is unclear?
  • How many recent products should be kept in the state?
  • Should context be kept when the user returns to a session later?

items.title: The problem
items.text:
Simple recommendation and search models work well at the start, but they have limits:

  • They understand simple relationships between users and products, but miss more complex patterns.
  • They understand product text by keywords only, not by meaning.
  • They struggle with Arabic text, which has many spellings, forms, and dialects.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
Deep Learning Models introduce more advanced models that understand users, products, and text more deeply. The roadmap describes three parts:

  • Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF): the same idea as collaborative filtering ("users similar to you bought this"), but using a neural network that can learn more complex patterns.
  • Transformer-based product embeddings: converting each product into a list of numbers that represents its meaning, so similar products have close numbers, even if their names are different.
  • BERT for Arabic text understanding: a language model trained on Arabic that understands the meaning of Arabic text, useful for search, tagging, and review analysis.

Example:

Case Simple model Deep learning model User searches "كريم للبشرة الناشفة" Looks for the exact words, may miss products written as "مرطب للبشرة الجافة" Understands that both mean the same thing Two serums with different names but similar use Treats them as unrelated Their embeddings are close, so they are recommended together Review: "تحفة، استخدمته يومين وطلعلي حبوب" May classify it as positive because of "تحفة" Understands that the meaning is negative

In short, deep learning models make recommendations, search, and text understanding smarter, especially for Arabic.

items.title: 2. Current System Status
items.text:
Based on the information available in this report:

  • GoCare already has a product recommendation system in production.
  • The roadmap plans simpler approaches first, such as rule-based recommendations and Collaborative Filtering.
  • The website supports Arabic and English, and product content and reviews are written in both.
  • It is not yet confirmed what computing resources (CPU or GPU) are available.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • Deep learning models should come after simpler models are in place and measured.
  • They need more data and more computing resources than the current models.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to improve the quality of recommendations, search, and text understanding, especially for Arabic content, once enough data is available.

Expected benefits:

  • More accurate recommendations: learning complex user preferences.
  • Better search: finding products by meaning, not only exact words.
  • Better Arabic understanding: supporting Automated Content Tagging and Sentiment Analysis.
  • Shared product representations: the same product embeddings can be reused by recommendations, search, Visual Search, and the chatbot.

Example:

With product embeddings, a user who likes a specific niacinamide serum can be recommended other serums with similar effects, even from different brands with different names.

Priority: Medium, according to the roadmap.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Team Lead / Client
items.text:
1. Which use case should come first?

Recommendations (NCF), product embeddings for search and similarity, or Arabic text understanding (BERT)?

2. What improvement would justify the extra cost?

For example, a clear increase in click-through or conversion compared to the simpler models.

3. Is there a budget for GPU resources?

Deep learning models often need GPUs for training, and sometimes for serving.

items.title: 4.2 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. How much interaction data is available for training NCF?
  2. Are product names and descriptions available in Arabic and English for embeddings and BERT?
  3. What computing resources are available for training and serving models?
  4. How are models currently deployed and monitored?
  5. Is there a labeled Arabic dataset, such as tagged products or labeled reviews, for fine-tuning BERT?

items.title: 4.3 Shared Question
items.text:
When should deep learning replace or extend the simpler models?

The team lead agrees on the success criteria, and the technical team compares the deep learning models with the simpler models on the same data before deciding.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Neural Collaborative Filtering

The system must train a neural network on user-product interactions to predict which products each user may like.

FR-02: Product embeddings

The system must create an embedding for each product using a Transformer model, based on its name, description, and attributes.

Example: two moisturizers for dry skin from different brands have close embeddings.

FR-03: Arabic text understanding

The system must use an Arabic-capable BERT model to understand Arabic product text, search queries, and reviews.

Example: "بشرة ناشفة" and "بشرة جافة" are understood as the same meaning.

FR-04: Comparison with existing models

Each deep learning model must be compared with the current or simpler model before it is used in production.

Proposed additional requirements (need confirmation):

  • FR-05: Reusing product embeddings in search, Visual Search, and the chatbot.
  • FR-06: Fine-tuning BERT on GoCare's own Arabic data.
  • FR-07: Regular retraining with new data.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Performance

Model responses must be fast enough for real-time use on the website.

2. Cost

Training and serving costs must be justified by the improvement in results.

3. Quality

Deep learning models must perform better than simpler models on agreed metrics before replacing them.

4. Maintainability

Models must be documented, versioned, and easy to retrain.

5. Reliability

If a deep learning model fails, the system must fall back to the simpler model.

Note: target values for response time, cost, and quality improvement must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status User Interactions Train Neural Collaborative Filtering Partly available (purchases); other interactions unconfirmed Product Names & Descriptions (Arabic and English) Create product embeddings and train BERT Exists on the website Product Attributes Improve embeddings Exists; completeness needs review Search Queries Improve search understanding Unconfirmed Labeled Arabic Data Fine-tune BERT Not available; needs to be prepared Computing Resources (GPU) Train and serve models Unconfirmed

Example:

If GoCare has only a few thousand interactions, a neural collaborative filtering model may perform worse than simple matrix factorization, because deep models need much more data.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
All three parts use well-known approaches:

  • Neural Collaborative Filtering can be built with standard deep learning libraries.
  • Product embeddings can start from pre-trained multilingual Transformer models, without training from scratch.
  • Arabic BERT models are publicly available and pre-trained on Arabic text, and can be fine-tuned on GoCare's data.

The recommended approach is to start with pre-trained models and fine-tune them, instead of training large models from scratch.

Initial assessment: technically feasible, but it requires more data, more computing resources, and more expertise than simpler models. It should come after the simpler models are in place and measured.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Enough interaction and text data.
  • GPU or cloud computing resources.
  • Simpler baseline models, such as Collaborative Filtering, for comparison.
  • Model Compression, to reduce the size and cost of the deep learning models.
  • The Analytics Dashboard, to measure the impact.
  • Collaboration between the Data, Backend, and Recommendation teams.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Data requirements

Deep models need much more data than simple models to perform well.

2. Cost

Training and serving deep models can be expensive.

3. Complexity

Deep models are harder to build, debug, explain, and maintain.

4. Arabic dialects

Pre-trained Arabic models may not fully understand local dialects and mixed Arabic-English text without fine-tuning.

Example:

If a deep learning model improves click-through by only 1% but doubles server costs, it may not be worth using in production.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text: The feature is not important at the moment.

items.title: 1. Feature Overview
items.text:
Demand Forecasting aims to predict how much of each product GoCare is expected to sell in the coming period, based on historical sales data, while taking seasons and trends into account.

The feature has three main parts:

  • Sales forecasting: predicting the expected sales quantity of each product for the coming weeks or months.
  • Seasonal and trend awareness: adjusting forecasts for seasons, holidays, and rising or falling trends.
  • Stock planning support: helping the team decide when and how much to restock, to reduce stockouts and overstock.

Example:

The system predicts that sunscreen sales will increase in summer, and that perfume sales will increase before Ramadan and Eid, so the team orders larger quantities early.

Note: unlike the recommendation features, this is a prediction and analytics feature for internal teams, mainly inventory and purchasing, rather than a feature shown to users.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare sells products across many categories, such as skin care, hair care, makeup, perfumes, personal care, and beauty devices.
  • The website runs seasonal and promotional offers, which affect sales volumes.
  • It is not yet confirmed how much sales history is stored, and for how long.
  • It is not yet confirmed whether stock levels and stockout periods are recorded.
  • It is not yet confirmed how stock is managed today, for example by GoCare directly or by each seller or brand.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • Forecast quality depends mainly on the amount and quality of sales history.
  • Promotions and stockouts must be recorded, otherwise the model may learn wrong patterns.
  • The way stock is managed decides who will use the forecasts and how.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to keep the right amount of stock for each product, so customers find what they want and less money is tied up in products that do not sell.

Expected benefits:

  • Fewer stockouts and lost sales.
  • Less overstock and fewer expired or unsold products.
  • Better planning for seasonal peaks, such as summer, Ramadan, Eid, and promotional events.
  • More data-driven purchasing decisions.

Example:

Instead of ordering the same quantity of sunscreen every month, the team orders more before summer and less in winter, based on the forecast.

Business Impact: High, according to the client's assessment.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Client
items.text:
1. Who will use the forecasts?

The inventory team, the purchasing team, sellers and brands on the platform, or management?

2. What forecast horizon is needed?

Next week, next month, or next season?

3. At what level should forecasts be made?

Per product, per category, per brand, or per city or warehouse?

4. How should forecasts be delivered?

A dashboard, a regular report, or automatic restock suggestions?

5. Which events affect sales the most?

For example: summer, Ramadan, Eid, White Friday, national holidays, or brand campaigns?

6. How is stock managed today?

Does GoCare hold the stock, or does each seller or brand manage their own stock?

items.title: 4.2 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. How far back does sales history go, and at what level (per order, per day, per product)?
  2. Are stock levels recorded over time, including periods when products were out of stock?
  3. Are promotions and discounts recorded with their dates?
  4. Are returns and cancellations recorded?
  5. Are new products, discontinued products, and product variants (e.g. sizes and shades) clearly identified?

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Product demand forecasting

The system must predict the expected sales quantity of each product for a defined future period.

Example: product A is expected to sell 300 units next month.

FR-02: Seasonal and event adjustments

The system must take seasons, holidays, and known events into account in the forecasts.

Example: perfume forecasts increase in the weeks before Eid.

FR-03: Trend detection

The system must detect products whose sales are rising or falling over time.

Example: a new serum shows steadily rising sales over the last eight weeks.

FR-04: Stockout and overstock alerts

The system must highlight products expected to run out soon, or that have more stock than expected demand.

Example: sunscreen stock is expected to run out in two weeks based on the summer forecast.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-05: Suggested restock quantities for each product.
  • FR-06: Forecasts per city or warehouse.
  • FR-07: A dashboard comparing forecasts with actual sales.
  • FR-08: Including planned promotions in the forecasts.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Forecast Accuracy

Forecasts must be accurate enough to support purchasing decisions, and their error must be measured regularly against actual sales.

2. Regular Updates

Forecasts must be refreshed regularly, for example weekly, as new sales data arrives.

3. Explainability

The team should understand the main reasons behind a forecast, such as a seasonal peak or a recent trend.

4. Scalability

The system must handle a growing number of products and categories.

5. Reliability

A failure in the forecasting pipeline must not affect the website or other systems.

Note: target values for forecast accuracy and update frequency must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Sales History Train the forecasting model Available in the product recommendation system; length of history unconfirmed Stock Levels Over Time Separate real demand from stockout periods Unconfirmed Promotions & Discounts Explain sales peaks caused by offers Unconfirmed Product Catalog & Categories Group products and forecast new products Exists on the website Returns & Cancellations Calculate real net demand Unconfirmed Event Calendar Account for Ramadan, Eid, and other seasons Not available; needs to be prepared Product Lifecycle (new / discontinued) Avoid forecasting discontinued products Unconfirmed

Example:

If a product was out of stock for two weeks, its sales during that time were zero, not because nobody wanted it, but because it was not available. If stock levels are not recorded, the model may wrongly learn that demand dropped.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can start with simple and well-known forecasting methods:

  • Baseline methods: moving averages and same-period-last-year comparisons.
  • Statistical time series models: such as Exponential Smoothing or ARIMA, which handle trends and seasonality.
  • Event adjustments: adding known events, such as Ramadan and Eid, which move each year in the Gregorian calendar.

Later, more advanced approaches can be tested, such as:

  • Machine Learning models (e.g. Gradient Boosting) that use features like price, promotions, category, and events.
  • Forecasting libraries designed for business time series with holidays and seasonality.

Initial assessment: technically feasible. Forecast quality depends mainly on having enough sales history, recorded promotions, and recorded stock levels.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Enough historical sales data, preferably more than one year.
  • Recorded stock levels and promotions.
  • An agreed list of important seasons and events.
  • Collaboration with the inventory and purchasing teams.
  • Collaboration between the Data, Backend, and Recommendation teams.
  • Coordination with the Analytics Dashboard feature, which can display forecasts.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Short sales history

If GoCare does not have at least one full year of data, the model cannot learn yearly seasons reliably.

2. Moving events

Ramadan and Eid move about 11 days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar, so simple yearly comparisons can be misleading.

3. New products

New products have no sales history, so their forecasts must rely on similar products in the same category.

4. Hidden demand

Stockouts and promotions can hide the real demand if they are not recorded.

Example:

If last year's Eid was in April and this year's Eid is in March, a model that only compares the same month of last year will predict the Eid peak in the wrong month.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. Not a priority for now

Demand Forecasting is not considered very important at the moment.

2. Not enough data

There is not enough customer and sales data yet to build reliable forecasts. As explained in this page, learning seasons such as summer, Ramadan, and Eid needs at least one full year of sales history.
