يريد النظام أن يتوقع زيادة مبيعات واقي الشمس في الصيف.

  • ما يحتاجه النظام: أن يرى أولًا بيانات المبيعات من صيف سابق واحد على الأقل.
  • الوضع الحالي: هذه البيانات غير متوفرة بعد، لذلك لن تكون التوقعات موثوقة، وتم تأجيل الميزة حتى تُجمع بيانات كافية.

items.title: The problem
items.text:
Product prices on GoCare are usually set once and changed manually. Meanwhile, competitors change their prices, and demand for products rises and falls. As a result:

  • Some products are priced higher than competitors and sell slowly.
  • Some products are discounted even when demand is already high.
  • The team cannot manually track competitor prices for thousands of products.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
Dynamic Pricing Optimization suggests a suitable price for each product, based on two main inputs:

  • Competitor price monitoring: tracking the prices of the same products in other stores.
  • Demand-based adjustments: adjusting the suggested price based on demand, such as high demand before Eid, low demand, or low stock.

These are price recommendations, reviewed and approved by the team before they are applied.

Example:

Product GoCare price Competitor price Demand Suggested action Sunscreen SPF 50 85 SAR 70 SAR Low Lower the price to around 75 SAR Perfume X 300 SAR 310 SAR High (before Eid) Keep the price, no discount needed Serum Y 120 SAR 120 SAR Very low, high stock Suggest a limited-time discount

In short:

  • Input: GoCare prices, competitor prices, sales and demand data, and stock levels.
  • Output: a suggested price, or price action, for each product.
  • Result: more competitive prices and better sales, without unnecessary discounts.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare runs offers such as free shipping on the first order in Riyadh, installment payments with Tabby and Tamara, and loyalty points.
  • Products come from different brands and sellers.
  • It is not yet confirmed who sets product prices today: GoCare, the sellers, or the brands.
  • It is not yet confirmed whether competitor prices are tracked in any way today.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • Who controls prices decides who will use the price recommendations.
  • Competitor price data must be collected before the feature can work.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to set competitive prices that increase sales and protect profit margins, based on data instead of manual guessing.

Expected benefits:

  • More competitive prices: fewer products priced far above competitors.
  • Better margins: avoiding unnecessary discounts on products with high demand.
  • Faster stock movement: suggesting discounts for slow-moving products with high stock.
  • Less manual work: the team does not need to check competitor prices by hand.

Example:

Instead of giving the same 20% discount on all perfumes before Eid, GoCare discounts only perfumes with low demand, and keeps the price of best-sellers.

Business Impact: High, according to the client's assessment.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Client
items.text:
1. Who sets and approves prices?

GoCare, the sellers, or the brands? Who will approve the suggested prices?

2. Which competitors should be monitored?

Which stores or websites, and for which product categories?

3. Are there pricing limits?

For example: minimum profit margin, maximum discount, or prices fixed by brand agreements?

4. How often can prices change?

Daily, weekly, or only during campaigns?

5. Should prices be applied automatically or manually?

Should the team approve every suggestion, or can small changes be applied automatically?

items.title: 4.2 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Is price history stored for each product?
  2. Is product cost stored, so profit margin can be calculated?
  3. Are sales, stock levels, and promotions recorded over time?
  4. Is there any existing source of competitor prices?
  5. Can product prices be updated through an API?

items.title: 4.3 Shared Question for the Client and Data Team
items.text:
How will competitor prices be collected?

The client confirms which competitors and products matter, and whether collecting their prices is allowed. The data team confirms the method, such as a pricing data provider or an approved data feed.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Competitor price monitoring

The system must collect and store competitor prices for matching products.

Example: the system records that the same sunscreen is sold at 70 SAR in another store.

FR-02: Product matching

The system must match GoCare products with the same products in competitor stores.

Example: "Sunscreen SPF 50, 50 ml" on GoCare is matched with the same product, brand, and size on another site.

FR-03: Price recommendations

The system must suggest a price, or a price action, for each product based on competitor prices, demand, and stock.

Example: lower the price, keep the price, or suggest a limited-time discount.

FR-04: Pricing rules

The system must respect pricing limits, such as minimum margin and maximum discount.

Example: the system never suggests a price below cost.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-05: A review screen to approve or reject price suggestions.
  • FR-06: Alerts when a competitor price changes significantly.
  • FR-07: Automatic application of small, approved price changes.
  • FR-08: Reports comparing sales before and after price changes.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Accuracy

Product matching and price suggestions must be accurate, since wrong prices directly affect revenue.

2. Data Freshness

Competitor prices must be updated often enough to be useful.

3. Control & Traceability

Every price change must be recorded, with who approved it and why.

4. Legal Compliance

Competitor price collection and pricing practices must follow applicable laws and the terms of the data sources.

5. Reliability

A failure in the pricing system must not change or break the prices shown on the website.

Note: target values for update frequency and matching accuracy must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Current Prices Compare with competitors Exists on the website Price History Learn how price affects sales Unconfirmed Product Cost Calculate margins and minimum price Unconfirmed Sales History Measure demand Available in the product recommendation system Stock Levels Adjust prices for low or high stock Unconfirmed Promotions Separate promotion effects from normal demand Unconfirmed Competitor Prices Main input for comparison Not available; source needs to be agreed

Example:

If product cost is not available, the system may suggest a lower price that is actually below cost, which would cause a loss.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can be rule-based:

  • Collect competitor prices for a limited set of key products.
  • Match products by brand, name, and size.
  • Apply clear pricing rules, such as "stay within 5% of the lowest competitor price, without going below the minimum margin".
  • Use demand and stock data to decide between lowering, keeping, or discounting the price.

Later, more advanced approaches can be tested, such as:

  • Price elasticity models: estimating how much sales change when the price changes.
  • Machine Learning models that combine demand forecasting, competitor prices, and seasonality.

Initial assessment: technically feasible, but it depends mainly on a reliable and allowed source of competitor prices, and on having product cost data.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• A reliable and allowed source of competitor prices.
  • Product cost and pricing rules.
  • Sales, stock, and price history.
  • The Demand Forecasting feature, which provides demand signals.
  • Collaboration with the pricing or commercial team, and with sellers if they control prices.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Competitor data access

Collecting competitor prices may be limited by website terms, technical blocks, or cost.

2. Product matching errors

Comparing different products, sizes, or versions leads to wrong suggestions.

3. Price wars

Automatically following competitor prices can lead to repeated price drops and lower margins.

4. Customer trust

Frequent price changes may reduce customer trust.

Example:

If a 50 ml product is matched with a 100 ml version on another site, the competitor price will look higher than it really is, and the suggestion will be wrong.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text: The feature has already been completed, and only testing remains.

items.title: 1. Feature Overview
items.text:
Model Compression is an internal technical improvement that reduces the size of GoCare's recommendation models by 30–50% using model quantization, enabling faster loading times and lower memory usage.

This is not a user-facing feature. Users will not see a new screen, but they may notice faster recommendations.

The improvement has three main parts:

  • Quantization: storing model weights with lower numerical precision (e.g. from 32-bit to 8-bit), which reduces model size.
  • Performance testing: measuring loading time, memory usage, and response time before and after compression.
  • Quality validation: making sure recommendation quality does not drop significantly after compression.

Example:

A recommendation model of 400 MB is compressed to about 200–280 MB. It loads faster when the service starts and uses less server memory, while giving nearly the same recommendations.

items.title: 2. Current System Status
items.text:
Based on the information available in this report:

  • GoCare runs a product recommendation system in production.
  • The size, format, and loading time of the current models are not yet confirmed.
  • It is not yet confirmed whether the models run on CPU or GPU servers.

What does this mean for the improvement?

  • The current models must be measured first, to know the actual gain from compression.
  • The best compression method depends on the model type and the server it runs on.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to make the recommendation system faster and cheaper to run.

Expected benefits:

  • Faster service startup and recommendation responses.
  • Lower memory usage and possibly lower server costs.
  • Easier scaling when the number of users grows.
  • Room to run more models, such as Visual Search, on the same servers.

Example:

If each model uses half the memory, the same server can run two models instead of one.

Priority: Medium, according to the roadmap.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Team Lead / Client
items.text:
1. What is the main goal of compression?

Faster responses, lower server costs, or freeing resources for new models?

2. How much quality loss is acceptable?

For example, is a 1–2% drop in recommendation accuracy acceptable in exchange for a 50% smaller model?

3. Which models should be compressed first?

All recommendation models, or only the largest ones?

items.title: 4.2 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Which models are used in production, and what are their sizes and formats?
  2. Do the models run on CPU or GPU?
  3. What are the current loading time, memory usage, and response time?
  4. Is there an offline evaluation dataset to compare recommendation quality before and after compression?
  5. How are models deployed, and can a compressed model be tested side by side with the current one?

items.title: 4.3 Shared Question
items.text:
How will we decide that a compressed model is good enough?

The team lead agrees on the acceptable quality and speed thresholds, and the technical team confirms they can be measured.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Compress recommendation models

The models must be compressed using quantization, reducing their size by 30–50%.

FR-02: Keep the same outputs format

The compressed models must return recommendations in the same format, so no changes are needed in other systems.

FR-03: Measure performance before and after

Size, loading time, memory usage, and response time must be measured for both versions.

FR-04: Validate recommendation quality

Recommendation quality must be compared between the original and compressed models.

Proposed additional requirements (need confirmation):

  • FR-05: The ability to quickly switch back to the original model if problems appear.
  • FR-06: A/B testing of the compressed model with real users before full rollout.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Performance

Loading time and memory usage must decrease noticeably after compression.

2. Quality

Recommendation quality must stay within the agreed acceptable limit.

3. Reliability

Replacing the model must not cause downtime in the recommendation service.

4. Maintainability

The compression steps must be documented and repeatable whenever models are retrained.

Note: target values for size reduction, speed, and acceptable quality loss must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Current Model Files Apply compression Exists in production Model Size & Format Choose the compression method Unconfirmed Current Performance Metrics Compare before and after Unconfirmed Evaluation Dataset Validate recommendation quality Unconfirmed Server Specifications Choose CPU or GPU optimizations Unconfirmed

Example:

Without an evaluation dataset, we cannot prove that the compressed model gives recommendations as good as the original one.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
Quantization is a standard and well-supported technique:

  • Post-training quantization: compressing an already trained model, without retraining. This is the fastest option.
  • Quantization-aware training: retraining the model with quantization in mind, if quality drops too much.

The method depends on the model type. For example, embedding-based recommendation models can often have their embeddings stored at lower precision with little quality loss.

Initial assessment: technically feasible, and usually low-risk, provided that the current models and an evaluation dataset are available.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Access to the production models and their training code.
  • An evaluation dataset and quality metrics.
  • A testing environment similar to production.
  • Collaboration with the Backend / DevOps team for deployment.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Quality loss

Some models may lose more accuracy than expected after compression.

2. Hardware support

Some quantized formats run faster only on specific hardware.

3. Limited gain

If the models are already small, the improvement may not be worth the effort.

4. Retraining process

If compression is not added to the training pipeline, it must be repeated manually every time models are retrained.

Example:

If a model is compressed by 50% but its response time does not improve on the current servers, the main gain will be lower memory only.

items.title: Assessment
items.text:
Importance: Medium to Low (for now)

  • This is an internal improvement, so users will not notice a big difference, and it does not directly increase sales.
  • Its real value depends on the current model sizes and server load, which are not measured yet.
  • Its importance increases if recommendations are slow, server costs are high, or heavier models such as Visual Search need to run on the same servers.

Suggestion: measure the current models first, and decide on compression based on the results.

items.title: Personalization Engine
items.text: Priority: Medium · Effort: High

items.title: The problem
items.text: Even with memory and saved preferences, the agent still answers every user in the same general way. It does not adapt its greeting, its content, or its tone to who the user is, how they behave, or what time it is.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
The Personalization Engine adapts the agent's responses to each user:

  • Personalized greetings and responses: greeting returning users by name, and referring to their recent activity.
  • Behavior-based content adaptation: adapting answers based on what the user usually browses or buys.
  • Time-of-day awareness: adapting suggestions to the time of day, such as morning or night routines.
  • User journey tracking: knowing where the user is in their shopping journey (e.g. new visitor, browsing, comparing, returning customer).
  • Adaptive response tone: adapting the tone and length of answers to the user's style.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Morning, returning user: Agent: Good morning, Sara! Your sunscreen from last month may be running low. Would you like to reorder it?

Night, new user: Agent: Welcome to GoCare! Are you looking for anything for your night routine?

items.title: 2. Why It Matters
items.text:
• Better engagement: personal conversations feel more natural and helpful.
  • Higher conversion: suggestions match the user's behavior and timing.
  • Repeat purchases: reminders based on past purchases encourage reordering.
  • Builds loyalty: users feel the assistant knows them.

items.title: Functional Requirements
items.text:
• FR-01: Personalized greetings and responses: the agent greets users by name and refers to relevant past activity.
  • FR-02: Behavior-based content adaptation: the agent adapts suggestions to the user's browsing and purchase behavior.
  • FR-03: Time-of-day awareness: the agent adapts suggestions to the current time of day.
  • FR-04: User journey tracking: the agent identifies the user's current stage in their shopping journey.
  • FR-05: Adaptive response tone: the agent adapts its tone and answer length to the user's communication style.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
• Privacy: personalization must not feel intrusive, and must only use data the user agreed to share.
  • Transparency: users should understand why they see personalized suggestions.
  • Performance: personalization must not noticeably slow down responses.
  • Fallback: if personalization data is missing, the agent answers normally.

items.title: 4. Technical Approach
items.text:
• User context builder: at the start of each conversation, build a small user context from the profile, preferences, long-term memory, and recent orders.
  • Prompt personalization: add this context to the system prompt, such as the user's name, language, tone, and recent purchases.
  • Journey stage: a simple rule-based classifier based on account age, number of orders, and recent activity (e.g. "new", "browsing", "returning customer").
  • Time awareness: pass the user's local time to the agent, and use simple rules for morning and night suggestions.
  • Recommendation integration: use the recommendation system to get personalized product suggestions for the user.
  • Tone adaptation: detect the user's style (e.g. short messages or casual language) and adjust the response style, within GoCare's brand voice.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• User Profiles & Authentication, User Preferences & Settings, and Conversation Memory Management.
  • Access to order and browsing history.
  • The recommendation system, for personalized product suggestions.

items.title: Risks
items.text:
• Feeling intrusive: too much personal detail can make users uncomfortable.
  • Wrong assumptions: the agent may personalize based on incorrect data.
  • Inconsistent brand voice: adapting tone too much may not fit GoCare's style.
  • More tokens: adding user context to each request increases cost.

items.title: 7. Open Questions
items.text:
• Which user data is the agent allowed to mention in conversations (e.g. past orders)?
  • Should personalization be optional, with a way for users to turn it off?
  • Is browsing history available to the agent, or only orders?

items.title: 1. Feature Overview
items.text:
Personalized Marketing aims to automatically create marketing campaigns for different customer segments on GoCare, instead of sending the same offer to all customers.

The feature has three main parts:

  • Customer segmentation: grouping customers based on their behavior and preferences (e.g. what they buy, how often, how much they spend, and whether they book salons).
  • Automated campaign creation: preparing a suitable message or offer for each segment automatically.
  • A/B testing: sending two versions of the same campaign to small groups, measuring which one performs better, then sending the better version to the rest of the segment.

Example:

Customers who often buy hair care products receive a notification about new hair care products, while customers who often book salons receive an offer on salon services.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare combines a beauty products store with salon booking, so customer behavior can include both purchases and bookings.
  • The website already runs general offers, such as free shipping on the first order in Riyadh, installment payments with Tabby and Tamara, and 1,000 points on registration.
  • It is not yet confirmed which customer behavior data is recorded (e.g. page views, clicks, searches, abandoned carts).
  • Campaigns will be sent as notifications.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • GoCare already runs promotions, so the feature can build on existing offers rather than start from scratch.
  • The feature depends heavily on behavior data, which must be confirmed first.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to increase sales and customer engagement by sending each customer group offers that match their interests, instead of general offers.

Expected benefits:

  • Higher response rates to campaigns.
  • Increased repeat purchases and bookings.
  • Less wasted marketing effort on offers that do not interest customers.
  • Data-driven decisions on which messages and offers work best, through A/B testing.

Example:

Instead of sending the same discount to all customers, GoCare sends a hair care offer only to customers interested in hair care, which is more likely to lead to a purchase.

Business Impact: High, according to the client's assessment.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Which customer behavior data is recorded (page views, clicks, searches, cart activity, purchases, bookings)?
  2. Is customer purchase and booking history stored and accessible?
  3. Are customers' marketing consent and contact preferences stored?
  4. Is there an existing integration with a notification service?
  5. Can campaign results (opens, clicks, purchases) be tracked back to each campaign?

items.title: 4.2 Shared Question for the Client and Data Team
items.text:
What data can be used to segment customers?

The client decides which customer attributes and behaviors should define segments, and the data team confirms which of them are actually recorded and can be used legally.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Customer segmentation

The system must group customers into segments based on their behavior and preferences.

Example: a segment of customers who bought hair care products in the last 60 days.

FR-02: Automated campaign creation

The system must prepare a suitable campaign for each segment, including the message and the offer.

Example: customers who often buy skin care products receive a notification about a new serum, with a related offer.

FR-03: A/B testing

The system must support sending two versions of a campaign to small test groups and comparing their results.

Example: version A offers 10% off, version B offers free shipping; the version with more purchases is sent to the rest of the segment.

FR-04: Campaign performance tracking

The system must track the results of each campaign, such as opens, clicks, and purchases.

FR-05: Campaign frequency limit

Each customer must receive a maximum of one campaign notification about every two weeks.

FR-06: Marketing team review

Every campaign must be reviewed and approved by the marketing team before it is sent.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-07: Product recommendations inside campaigns, based on the recommendation system.
  • FR-08: Unsubscribe option in every campaign.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Scalability

The system must handle growth in the number of customers and campaigns without significant delays.

2. Reliability

Campaigns must not be sent twice to the same customer, and failures must be logged and retried safely.

3. Privacy & Security

Customer data must be used only with marketing consent, and every campaign must allow customers to unsubscribe, in line with data protection and marketing regulations in Saudi Arabia.

4. Measurability

Every campaign must be trackable so its results can be measured and compared.

5. Statistical Reliability

A/B test results must be based on enough data to make the difference between versions meaningful, not random.

Note: target values for sending speed, delivery rates, and test sample sizes must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Purchase History Segment customers by what they buy Available in the product recommendation system Booking History Segment salon customers Unconfirmed Browsing Behavior (views, clicks, searches) Understand customer interests Unconfirmed Cart Activity Identify abandoned carts Unconfirmed Customer Profile Basic segmentation (e.g. city, registration date) Unconfirmed Marketing Consent Send campaigns legally Unconfirmed Contact Channels Deliver campaigns Notifications (agreed in the meeting) Campaign Results Measure performance and run A/B tests Not collected yet

Example:

If only purchase history is available, the system can segment customers by what they bought, but cannot target customers who showed interest in a product without buying it.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can be built with simple, rule-based segments:

  • Segments defined by clear rules (e.g. last purchase date, number of orders, total spending, product categories).
  • Campaign templates prepared for each segment.
  • A simple A/B testing setup that randomly splits a segment into test groups.

Later, more advanced approaches can be tested, such as:

  • Clustering: discovering customer segments automatically from behavior data.
  • RFM analysis: segmenting customers by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary value.
  • AI-generated content: generating campaign messages for each segment, reviewed before sending.

Initial assessment: technically feasible, provided that customer behavior data, marketing consent, and a sending channel are available.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Customer behavior and purchase data.
  • A notification service and integration with it.
  • Marketing consent data.
  • Collaboration with the marketing team on offers and approvals.
  • Collaboration between the Backend, Data, and Recommendation teams.
  • Coordination with the Churn Prediction feature, which handles discount codes for inactive customers, so the same customer does not receive duplicate messages.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Missing behavior data

If browsing and cart activity are not recorded, segmentation will be limited to purchases only.

2. Customer fatigue

Sending too many campaigns may lead customers to unsubscribe or ignore messages.

3. Legal and consent requirements

Sending campaigns without proper consent can create legal and reputation risks.

4. Small test groups

If segments are small, A/B test results may not be reliable.

Example:

If a segment has only 50 customers, splitting it into two groups of 25 may not show a meaningful difference between the two versions.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. Campaigns are sent as notifications only

Personalized campaigns will be delivered to customers as notifications only. Other channels, such as email, SMS, and WhatsApp, are not part of this feature for now.

2. Limited frequency

Each customer receives a maximum of one campaign notification about every two weeks, to avoid customer fatigue.

3. Discount codes for inactive customers move to Churn Prediction

Win-back offers, such as discount codes for customers who stopped buying, will be handled by the Churn Prediction feature instead of this feature. Personalized Marketing focuses on sending relevant offers and products to active customer segments.

4. Campaigns are reviewed by the marketing team

Campaigns are not sent automatically. The marketing team reviews and approves every campaign before it is sent.

5. All customer segments are included

The feature covers all customer segments, such as new customers, frequent buyers, and salon customers.

مثال:

عميلتان لكل منهما سلوك شراء مختلف.

  • عميلة تشتري منتجات العناية بالشعر كثيرًا: يصلها إشعار واحد عن منتجات العناية بالشعر الجديدة، ولا يصلها أي إشعار حملة آخر خلال الأسبوعين التاليين.
  • عميلة لم تشترِ أي شيء منذ ثلاثة أشهر: لا تحصل على كود خصم من هذه الميزة، وبدلًا من ذلك تتولى ميزة Churn Prediction التعامل معها.

items.title: The problem
items.text:
Customers leave reviews and comments on GoCare products and services, in Arabic and English. For example:

"The cream is very good and the texture is light."

"Caused redness on my skin after two days."

"الكريم حلو بس العبوة وصلت مكسورة"

When there are only a few reviews, the team can read them one by one. When there are thousands, it becomes impossible to read them all, and real problems with a product can be missed until they become serious.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
Sentiment Analysis reads customer reviews and feedback automatically and:

  • Detects the sentiment of each review: positive, negative, or neutral.
  • Detects the topic of the review, such as quality, side effects, packaging, delivery, price, or scent.
  • Highlights product issues by grouping negative reviews about the same problem and alerting the team.

For the reviews above, the system produces:

Review Sentiment Topic The cream is very good and the texture is light. Positive Product quality Caused redness on my skin after two days. Negative Side effects الكريم حلو بس العبوة وصلت مكسورة Mixed Product quality (positive), packaging (negative)

In short:

  • Input: customer reviews and feedback (free text).
  • Output: sentiment and topic for each review, plus alerts for repeated problems.
  • Result: the team finds product issues early, before they affect many customers.

items.title: Why Arabic and English
items.text: GoCare customers write in Arabic, English, or a mix of both, and Arabic reviews are often written in dialect (e.g. Saudi or Egyptian) rather than formal Arabic. The system must understand all of these.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare has a ratings feature, shown on salons and products.
  • Almost all salons had no ratings at the time of review.
  • It is not yet confirmed how many product reviews and comments exist.
  • It is not yet confirmed whether other feedback sources exist, such as customer service messages, chatbot conversations, or return reasons.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • The feature depends on having enough reviews and feedback to analyze.
  • If product reviews are few, other feedback sources, such as chatbot conversations and return reasons, may be more useful at the start.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to discover product and service problems early, and understand what customers like and dislike, without reading every review manually.

Expected benefits:

  • Early problem detection: spotting issues, such as a batch of damaged products or a product causing irritation, before they spread.
  • Better product decisions: knowing which products customers love and which ones they complain about.
  • Better customer service: responding quickly to negative feedback.
  • Better recommendations: avoiding recommending products with many recent complaints.

Example:

If many reviews of the same moisturizer mention "redness" or "irritation" in one week, the system alerts the team, who can check the product or contact the supplier quickly.

Business Impact: Moderate, according to the client's assessment.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. How many product reviews and comments are stored, and in which languages?
  2. Are reviews linked to the product, the seller, and the order date?
  3. Are other feedback sources stored, such as chatbot conversations or return reasons?
  4. Are star ratings stored together with the review text?
  5. Can results be stored and shown in the Analytics Dashboard?

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Sentiment detection

The system must classify each review as positive, negative, neutral, or mixed.

Example: "Caused redness on my skin" is classified as negative.

FR-02: Topic detection

The system must identify what each review is about.

Example: "The bottle arrived broken" is about packaging.

FR-03: Arabic and English support

The system must understand reviews in Arabic, English, or a mix of both, including common dialect words.

Example: "حلو جدًا" and "very nice" are both classified as positive.

FR-04: Product issue alerts

The system must alert the team when negative reviews about the same problem increase for a product.

Example: five reviews mentioning irritation for the same product within one week trigger an alert.

FR-05: Results in the Analytics Dashboard

The analysis results must be shown in the Analytics Dashboard, inside the existing Admin Dashboard.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-06: A summary per product showing its main strengths and complaints.
  • FR-07: Analysis of chatbot conversations and return reasons.
  • FR-08: Sharing product feedback summaries with sellers and brands.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Accuracy

Sentiment and topic results must be accurate enough to trust, and accuracy must be measured on a set of manually labeled reviews.

2. Dialect Support

The system must handle Arabic dialects and mixed Arabic and English, not only formal Arabic.

3. Timeliness

New reviews must be analyzed quickly enough for alerts to be useful, for example daily.

4. Privacy & Security

Customer names and personal information in reviews must be protected, in line with data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.

5. Reliability

If the analysis service fails, reviews must still be saved and shown on the website normally.

Note: target values for accuracy and analysis frequency must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Product Reviews & Comments Main input for analysis Unconfirmed (amount unknown) Star Ratings Support sentiment detection Feature exists; amount unconfirmed Salon Reviews Analyze salon feedback No ratings yet Review Details (product, seller, date) Group issues by product and time Unconfirmed Chatbot Conversations (optional) Extra feedback source Unconfirmed Return Reasons (optional) Extra feedback source Unconfirmed Manually Labeled Reviews Test and measure accuracy Not available; needs to be prepared

Example:

If a product has a 5-star rating but the text says "the bottle arrived broken", the star rating alone hides a packaging problem. This is why the review text must be analyzed, not only the stars.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can use existing language models:

  • Multilingual sentiment models: pre-trained models that support Arabic and English.
  • Large Language Models (LLMs): reading each review and returning its sentiment and topic, choosing from a fixed list of topics.
  • Simple alert rules: for example, an alert when negative reviews about the same topic for one product exceed a set number within a week.

Later, the system can be improved by:

  • Fine-tuning a model on GoCare's own labeled reviews, including local dialects.
  • Automatic summaries of the main complaints per product.

Initial assessment: technically feasible with current multilingual models. The main questions are whether there are enough reviews, and how well the models handle local dialects.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Enough customer reviews and feedback.
  • Reviews linked to products, sellers, and dates.
  • An agreed list of topics to detect.
  • A set of manually labeled reviews to measure accuracy.
  • Collaboration between the Data, Backend, and Recommendation teams, and the product and customer service teams.
  • Coordination with the Analytics Dashboard feature, which can display the results.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Few reviews

If most products have few or no reviews, the analysis will have limited value at the start.

2. Dialects and mixed language

Reviews may use dialect words, spelling mistakes, emojis, or a mix of Arabic and English.

3. Sarcasm and mixed opinions

Some reviews are sarcastic, or praise one aspect and criticize another, which is harder to classify.

4. Fake or spam reviews

Fake positive or negative reviews can distort the results.

Example:

The review "تحفة، استخدمته يومين وطلعلي حبوب" uses a positive word ("تحفة") sarcastically, while the real meaning is negative. Simple models may classify it wrongly, which is why accuracy must be tested on real GoCare reviews.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. The feature is important

Sentiment Analysis is considered an important feature for GoCare, since it helps the team discover product problems early and understand what customers like and dislike.

2. Not for now

The feature will not be built at the moment, because there is currently not a large number of customer reviews to analyze. It stays in the plan, and can start when the number of reviews increases.

3. Source: comments on the website

The analysis uses the customer comments written on the GoCare website.

4. Focus on negative feedback

The feature focuses on all negative comments, to find product problems and complaints.

5. Results shown in the Analytics Dashboard

The analysis results are shown in the Analytics Dashboard, inside the existing Admin Dashboard.

items.title: 1. Feature Overview
items.text:
Skincare Routine Advisor aims to help GoCare users build a complete skin care, hair care, or body care routine from the store's products, based on their skin, hair, or body care needs, instead of choosing products one by one without knowing what fits together.

The feature has three main parts:

  • Routine builder: suggesting the right products for each routine step based on the user's skin or hair type and concerns (e.g. cleanser, serum, moisturizer, and sunscreen for skin; shampoo, conditioner, mask, and serum for hair).
  • Product sequencing: showing the correct order of use, separating morning and night steps where relevant, and avoiding products that should not be used together.
  • Seasonal adjustments: adapting the routine to the season, such as a lighter moisturizer and stronger sunscreen in summer, or more hydrating hair products in winter.

Examples:

  • If a user has oily, acne-prone skin, the system may suggest a morning routine of a gel cleanser, a niacinamide serum, a light gel moisturizer, and an oil-free SPF 50 sunscreen.
  • If a user has dry, frizzy hair, the system may suggest a moisturizing shampoo, a deep conditioner, a weekly hair mask, and an anti-frizz serum.

All suggested products come from GoCare's store.

The feature is offered through the chatbot: the AI Agent asks the user which routine she wants (skin, hair, or body care), asks about her type and concerns, and presents the routine within the conversation.

Product selection is handled by the recommendation system.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare's store includes product categories such as skin care, hair care, makeup, personal care, body care, men's care, and beauty devices.
  • Products are already tagged with their routine step (e.g. cleanser, serum, shampoo). It is not yet confirmed whether they are tagged with skin or hair type and key ingredients.
  • The existing product recommendation system can already suggest related products.
  • The AI Agent team already has ongoing work related to routines in the chatbot.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • The products needed for skin, hair, and body care routines already exist in the store.
  • The main question is whether product data is detailed enough to build reliable routines.
  • Part of the logic may already exist or be planned in the AI Agent work, so scope must be aligned before starting.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to help users choose the right products for their skin or hair, increase confidence in their purchases, and increase the number of products bought together.

Expected benefits:

  • Easier product selection for users who don't know what fits their skin or hair.
  • Higher average order value, since users buy a full routine instead of a single product.
  • Encouraging repeat purchases when routine products run out.
  • Building trust in GoCare as a source of beauty advice.

Example:

Instead of buying a shampoo only, the user sees a full hair routine for their hair type and adds three or four matching products to the cart in one step.

Business Impact: High, according to the client's assessment.

items.title: 4. Functional Requirements
items.text:
The functions the system must be able to perform.

FR-01: Choose routine type

The chatbot must first ask the user which routine she wants: skin care, hair care, or body care.

Example: the chatbot asks "Which routine are you looking for?" with three options: skin, hair, or body care.

FR-02: Collect skin, hair, or body care profile

Based on the chosen routine type, the system must collect the user's skin type, hair type, or body care needs, and her main concerns.

Example: for skin, the user selects "oily" and "acne"; for hair, the user selects "dry" and "frizz".

FR-03: Build a routine based on the profile

The system must define the routine steps that fit the user's profile.

Example: oily skin gets a morning routine of cleanser, serum, light moisturizer, and sunscreen; dry hair gets a routine of moisturizing shampoo, conditioner, and a weekly mask.

FR-04: Recommend products for each step

The system must suggest suitable, in-stock store products for each routine step.

Example: for the shampoo step, the system suggests a moisturizing shampoo tagged for dry hair.

FR-05: Product sequencing

The system must show products in the correct order of use and avoid combining products that should not be used together.

Example: the system does not place two strong exfoliating products in the same skin routine.

FR-06: Seasonal adjustments

The system must adjust routine recommendations according to the season.

Example: in summer, the system prefers lighter moisturizers and higher SPF sunscreens; in winter, more hydrating hair products.

FR-07: Routine API for the chatbot

The recommendation system must provide an API that the AI Agent can use to get routine products during conversations.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-08: "Add full routine to cart" button.
  • FR-09: "Complete your routine" section on product pages and in the cart.
  • FR-10: Saving the user's skin and hair profiles in their account for future recommendations.
  • FR-11: A clear disclaimer that recommendations are cosmetic advice, not medical advice.

items.title: 5. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Performance

Routine results must appear quickly in the chatbot after the user answers the questions.

Example: the routine appears in the conversation without a noticeable delay after the last answer.

2. Reliability

If the routine service fails, the rest of the store must keep working normally.

Example: product pages still load even if the "complete your routine" section is unavailable.

3. Safety & Responsibility

Recommendations must stay within cosmetic advice, avoid medical claims, and show a disclaimer where needed.

4. Privacy & Security

Skin and hair profile data must be stored and used only with the user's consent, in line with data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.

5. Recommendation Quality

Routine rules and product matches must be reviewed for accuracy through a medical consultation before launch.

Note: target values for response time and recommendation accuracy must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 6. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Product Catalog Know which products can be recommended Exists in the store Product Categories Group products by type Exists on the website Skin / Hair Type per Product Match products to user profiles Unconfirmed Ingredients Check product conflicts Unconfirmed (structured or free text?) Routine Step per Product Place each product in the right step Available Stock Availability Avoid recommending unavailable products Unconfirmed Routine Rules Define steps, order, and conflicts for skin, hair, and body care Based on common skincare rules (from lightest to heaviest); to be reviewed through a medical consultation User Skin / Hair Profile Personalize routines Not collected yet Purchase History (optional) Improve recommendations and suggest refills Available in the product recommendation system

Example:

If products are not tagged with hair type, the system cannot tell whether a shampoo is suitable for dry or oily hair, and the routine would be unreliable.

Therefore, product data must be reviewed first, and missing attributes added before building the feature.

items.title: 7. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can be built as a Rule-Based Recommendation System:

  • A routine template for each skin type, hair type, and body care need defines the required steps.
  • Products are filtered by skin or hair type, routine step, and stock.
  • Conflict rules remove products that should not be used together.
  • Products are ranked by sales, ratings, or price range.
  • Seasonal rules adjust the routine based on the current month.

The same logic is exposed as an API, so it can be used by the AI Agent and at checkout.

Later, more advanced approaches can be tested, such as:

  • Content-Based Filtering: matching products to users based on product attributes.
  • Collaborative Filtering: suggesting products bought by users with similar profiles.

Initial assessment: feasibility depends mainly on product data quality. If products are tagged with skin or hair type, ingredients, and routine step, the feature is technically feasible. If not, data preparation will be the largest part of the work.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Product data with skin or hair type and ingredients (routine step is already available).
  • Common skincare rules for the order of use (from lightest to heaviest), reviewed through a medical consultation.
  • Alignment with the AI Agent team on the existing routine work.
  • Collaboration between the Backend, Frontend, Data, and Recommendation teams.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Incomplete product data

Many products may be missing skin or hair type or ingredients information.

2. Accuracy of routine rules

Wrong combinations or order of use could harm user trust or cause skin or scalp irritation.

3. Medical boundary

Users may describe skin or scalp conditions that need a doctor, not product recommendations.

4. Overlap with existing work

Building the same logic twice in the chatbot and the recommendation system wastes effort and may give users different answers.

Example:

If the chatbot shows one order of use and the checkout shows another for the same user, users will lose trust in both. This is why both must use the same recommendation logic.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. The routine is built in the chatbot

The routine feature will be offered through the chatbot. The AI Agent asks the user about her needs and presents the routine in the conversation, while the recommendation system selects the products for each step.

2. Routines cover skin care, hair care, and body care

In addition to skin care and hair care, the feature will also support body care routines.

3. Order of use for all routine types

The system shows the correct order of use for skin care, hair care, and body care products.

Routine type Order of use Skin care Cleanser, toner, serum, moisturizer, sunscreen Hair care Shampoo, conditioner, mask, serum Body care Shower gel, scrub, body lotion

4. Order of use appears in two places

  • In the chatbot: when the user asks how to use her products, or in which order, the chatbot shows the correct order of use.
  • At checkout (if the cost is low): a small "How to use your products" card lists the products in the user's cart in the correct order of use.

Rules for both places:

  • The checkout card is for information only, and must not block or slow down the checkout.
  • The order of use can also be shown on the order confirmation page or in the order email.
  • Products without a known routine step are shown at the end, instead of being placed in the wrong order.
  • The chatbot and checkout must use the same ordering rules, so the user always sees the same order.

items.title: 1. Feature Overview
items.text:
Smart Salon Services aims to help GoCare users easily find suitable salon services, instead of manually searching through a large number of salons and services.

The recommendation system relies on three main factors:

  • User preferences: e.g. interest in hair care or skin care services.
  • Booking history: services the user has previously booked through GoCare.
  • Location: suggesting services at salons near the user.

Recommendations are also linked to the booking system already on the website, making it easy to book the suggested services.

Example:

If a user is interested in hair care, has booked a Hair Spa service twice, and lives in Al Olaya, Riyadh, the system may suggest a Hair Treatment service at a nearby salon.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare has a salons section for searching salons and booking their services, with 43 salons at the time of review.
  • Salons are grouped into 12 categories.
  • Each salon shows its operating status (open or closed), as well as a ratings section.
  • The ratings feature exists, but almost all salons had no ratings at the time of review.
  • The website combines a beauty products store with a salon booking system.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • The booking system already exists; the task is to integrate with it rather than build a new one.
  • The existing service categories can be used to generate recommendations.
  • Ratings data is currently not enough to rely on.
  • Having the store and salons on one platform allows cross-recommendations between products and services in the future.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to help users reach salon services that fit their needs, improve the GoCare experience, and increase booking completion.

Expected benefits:

  • Less time spent searching for services.
  • Higher likelihood of booking recommended services.
  • Encouraging users to return to GoCare.
  • Helping salons reach customers interested in their services.

Example:

Instead of browsing 43 salons, the system can show three services related to the user's interests and location, making it easier to choose a service and complete the booking.

Business Impact: High, according to the client's assessment.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Client
items.text:
1. Where will recommendations appear?

On the homepage, the salons page, inside a specific salon's page, or during search?

2. Do price, salon status, and offers affect recommendations?

For example, should we recommend services at salons that are currently closed? Should discounted services get priority?

3. What happens when a recommendation is clicked?

Does the user go to the salon page, or directly to the booking process?

items.title: 4.2 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Does the current booking system provide an API that the recommendation system can use?
  2. Is users' booking history stored and accessible?
  3. Are salon locations stored as geographic coordinates, or only by city and area names?
  4. Is available booking slot data stored and accessible?
  5. Is every service linked to its correct category?

items.title: 4.3 Shared Question for the Client and Data Team
items.text:
What exactly counts as user preferences and activity history?

Should recommendations rely on past bookings only, or also include searches, salons the user viewed, favorites, and product purchases?

The data team must also confirm that this information is actually recorded in GoCare.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
The functions the recommendation system must be able to perform.

FR-01: Recommendations based on user preferences

The system must suggest services related to the user's recorded interests.

Example: if the user is interested in hair care, the system can suggest Hair Spa and Hair Treatment.

FR-02: Use of booking history

The system must take services the user previously booked into account when ranking recommendations.

Example: if the user has booked Hair Spa more than once, hair care services may get higher priority.

FR-03: Location-based recommendations

The system must provide recommendations based on the location the user enters herself.

Example: if the user selects Al Olaya in Riyadh, salons in or near that district can be prioritized.

FR-04: Integration with the booking system

Recommended services must be linked to GoCare's current booking system.

Example: the user clicks a recommended Hair Spa service, views its details, and picks an available time slot.

FR-05: Recommendations for new users

Users with no booking history must receive general salon recommendations.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-06: Show recommended service details, such as price, salon name, location, and operating status.
  • FR-07: Do not show cancelled or non-bookable services as available.
  • FR-08: Support future cross-recommendations between store products and salon services.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Performance

Recommendations must load at a suitable speed without affecting website performance.

Example: loading recommendations must not delay the homepage content from appearing.

2. Scalability

The system must handle growth in users, salons, and services without significant performance degradation.

3. Reliability

A failure in the recommendation system must not stop the website's core functions.

Example: if recommendations fail, the user can still search for salons and complete bookings.

4. Privacy & Security

User data, especially booking history and location, must be protected and used according to the appropriate permissions and consent, in line with data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.

5. Recommendation Quality

The relevance of recommended services to user interests must be evaluated, and result quality improved.

Note: target values for response time, availability, and concurrent users must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status User Preferences Know the user's interests Unconfirmed Booking History Know which services the user booked before Unconfirmed Service Catalog Know which services can be recommended Visible on the website; needs review Service Categories Identify similar services Available Salon Locations Suggest nearby salons when the user enters her location Storage method unconfirmed Service Availability Confirm the service can be booked Unconfirmed Prices & Promotions Consider prices and discounts Unconfirmed User Ratings Improve recommendation quality Not enough ratings currently Product Purchase History Cross-recommendations between the store and salons Reported as available in the product recommendation system

Example:

If the system knows the user is interested in hair care, but services are not correctly linked to their categories, it cannot reliably identify Hair Care services.

Therefore, the data must be reviewed and confirmed complete before choosing how to build the recommendation system.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can be built as a Rule-Based Recommendation System using a set of simple rules, without the need for complex Machine Learning models.

Example rules:

  • Prioritize services related to the user's interests.
  • Use the user's previous booking history.
  • Prefer salons close to the user.
  • Exclude services that cannot be booked.

As more data becomes available, more advanced approaches can be tested, such as:

  • Content-Based Filtering: recommending services similar to the user's interests.
  • Collaborative Filtering: using behavior patterns of similar users.

Reusing the current product recommendation system can also be studied, if some of its components are reusable.

Initial assessment: the feature is technically feasible in principle, provided that data availability and integration with the booking system are confirmed.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Availability of user and service data.
  • An API for integrating with the current booking system.
  • Availability of salon location data.
  • Collaboration between the Backend, Frontend, and Recommendation teams.
  • Coordination with the AI Agent team, since the chatbot can use the recommendation system to suggest services during conversations.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Sparse data

New users may have no booking history, and the ratings currently available are not enough.

2. Incomplete service data

Some services may be missing important information such as price, category, or location.

3. Slot availability

A service may suit the user, but have no available slots to book.

4. Location privacy

Some users may not enter their location.

Example:

If a salon's exact location is not available, the system cannot calculate the distance between it and the user. In this case, the city or area can be used instead of distance, as agreed.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

  • Recommend services, not salons: by default, the system recommends salon services, such as Hair Spa or Hair Treatment, instead of recommending whole salons.
  • Salon recommendations when location is entered: if the user enters her location herself, the system can also recommend nearby salons that offer these services.
  • New users: users with no booking history receive general salon recommendations.
  • Number of recommendations: the system shows 3 recommendations.

  • إذا أدخلت موقعها بنفسها: تظهر لها أيضًا الصالونات القريبة التي تقدم هذه الخدمات، مثل Salon A – العليا – على بُعد كيلومترين.

items.title: The problem
items.text: Many beauty purchases are influenced by other people: influencers on social media, friends, and family. However, GoCare's recommendations today are based only on the user's own behavior and on product attributes, not on the people the user trusts.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
Social Recommendations recommend products based on people. The roadmap describes two types:

  • Influencer suggestions: showing products used or recommended by beauty influencers.
  • Friend-based recommendations: showing products that the user's friends bought or liked, with their permission.

Example:

Type What the user sees Influencer suggestions "Products used by [influencer name] in her skin care routine" Friend-based recommendations "Your friend Sara added this serum to her favorites"

In short, the feature adds a social layer to recommendations, based on trust in real people.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare has user accounts and a favorites (wishlist) feature.
  • There is no friends or followers system on the website.
  • It is not yet confirmed whether GoCare works with influencers or has influencer partnerships.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • Friend-based recommendations need a new social system, which is a large change.
  • Influencer suggestions may be simpler to start with, if GoCare has influencer partnerships.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to increase trust and sales by using recommendations from people that users trust.

Expected benefits:

  • More trust: users trust products recommended by people they follow.
  • Higher conversion: influencer and friend recommendations often lead to purchases.
  • Marketing value: influencer collections can be part of marketing campaigns.
  • Engagement: users may return to see what friends and influencers like.

Example:

An influencer collection page showing her full skin care routine can drive many sales during a campaign.

Priority: Long-term vision, according to the roadmap.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Client
items.text:
1. Does GoCare work with influencers?

Are there existing partnerships, and can influencers create their own product lists?

2. Should there be a friends or followers system?

Is this part of GoCare's long-term plan?

3. Which should come first?

Influencer suggestions or friend-based recommendations?

4. How should privacy work?

Should users choose to share their purchases or favorites, or should everything be private by default?

items.title: 4.2 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Can new data such as influencer lists and friend connections be stored?
  2. Is there a way to link social media accounts?
  3. Are favorites and purchases stored in a way that can be shared with permission?

items.title: 4.3 Shared Question for the Client and Data Team
items.text:
What can be shared, and with whom?

The client decides the privacy rules, and the data team confirms how to store and enforce them.

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Influencer collections

The system must allow showing product lists recommended by influencers.

FR-02: Influencer-based recommendations

The system must recommend influencer products to users interested in similar products.

FR-03: Friend connections

The system must allow users to connect with friends, with their consent.

FR-04: Friend-based recommendations

The system must show products that friends chose to share, such as favorites or purchases.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-05: Privacy settings for what each user shares.
  • FR-06: Tracking sales from influencer collections.
  • FR-07: Influencer discount codes connected to their collections.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Privacy

Nothing about a user's purchases or favorites must be shown to others without clear consent, in line with data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.

2. Transparency

Paid influencer recommendations must be clearly marked as advertising.

3. Performance

Social recommendations must not slow down the website.

4. Moderation

Shared content must be reviewable to prevent misuse.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text: Data Purpose Status Influencer Product Lists Influencer suggestions Not available Influencer Partnerships Know which influencers to include Unconfirmed Friend Connections Friend-based recommendations Not available User Sharing Consent Respect privacy Not available Favorites & Purchases Content to share Available, but private

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
• Influencer suggestions are relatively simple: influencer product lists can be stored and shown as collections, and recommended to users with similar interests.
  • Friend-based recommendations require a new social system: friend connections, privacy settings, and sharing controls.

Initial assessment: influencer suggestions are technically feasible with limited effort. Friend-based recommendations are feasible but require a large product and privacy design effort.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Influencer partnerships and content.
  • A social system and privacy design for friend-based recommendations.
  • Collaboration with the marketing team.
  • Collaboration between the Backend, Frontend, and Recommendation teams.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Privacy concerns

Users may not want others to know what they buy, especially personal care products.

2. Small social network

Friend-based recommendations only work if many users connect with friends.

3. Advertising rules

Paid influencer content must follow advertising regulations.

4. Influencer reliability

An influencer's reputation can affect GoCare's brand.

Example:

If a user's purchase of a personal care product is shown to their friends without clear consent, it can seriously damage trust in GoCare.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. Important, but not a high priority

Social Recommendations is considered important, but not very important at the moment.

2. Monthly viral products by the marketing team

Instead of building influencer or friend systems, the marketing team will search every month for products that are viral on social media, and add them to the website. The list is updated every month.

مثال:

في بداية كل شهر، يبحث فريق التسويق في مواقع التواصل الاجتماعي عن منتجات التجميل الرائجة.

  • ما يجده الفريق: مثلًا، سيروم معيّن ينتشر بشكل واسع على تيك توك وإنستغرام هذا الشهر.
  • ما يفعله الفريق: يضيفه إلى قسم «الأكثر رواجًا هذا الشهر» في موقع GoCare، لكي يجده العملاء ويشتروه بسهولة.
  • في الشهر التالي: يحدّث الفريق القائمة بالمنتجات الرائجة الجديدة.

items.title: User Preferences & Settings
items.text: Priority: Medium · Effort: Medium

items.title: The problem
items.text: Every user has different preferences: some prefer Arabic, some English; some like a formal tone, others a casual one; some only buy certain brands or within a certain budget. Today, the agent does not store these preferences, so users must repeat them, and the agent cannot adapt its answers.

items.title: What the feature does
items.text:
The feature stores and uses each user's preferences:

  • Language preference: Arabic or English.
  • Notification preferences: which alerts the user wants, such as price alerts.
  • Communication style: formal or casual.
  • Product category interests: such as skin care, hair care, or perfumes.
  • Price range preferences: the user's usual budget.
  • Brand preferences: brands the user likes, or wants to avoid.

items.title: Example
items.text:
A user tells the agent once: "I prefer to talk in Arabic, keep it casual, and my budget is under 150 SAR."

In every future conversation, the agent answers in Arabic, uses a friendly tone, and recommends products under 150 SAR first.

items.title: 2. Why It Matters
items.text:
• Less repetition: users do not have to repeat their preferences.
  • More relevant results: products match the user's budget, brands, and interests.
  • Better experience: the agent talks in the user's preferred language and style.
  • Fewer unwanted notifications: users only receive the alerts they chose.

items.title: Functional Requirements
items.text:
• FR-01: Language preference storage: the agent saves and uses the user's preferred language.
  • FR-02: Notification preferences: users choose which notifications they receive.
  • FR-03: Communication style preference: the agent adapts between formal and casual tones.
  • FR-04: Product category interests: the agent saves categories the user is interested in and prioritizes them.
  • FR-05: Price range preferences: the agent saves the user's budget and uses it to filter or rank products.
  • FR-06: Brand preferences: the agent saves preferred and avoided brands.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
• User control: users can view, change, or reset their preferences at any time.
  • Privacy: preferences are stored securely and only used for this user.
  • Performance: loading preferences must not slow down responses.

items.title: 4. Technical Approach
items.text:
• Preferences store: a preferences table or document linked to the user ID, with fields such as language, tone, categories, price_min, price_max, preferred_brands, avoided_brands, and notifications.
  • Two ways to set preferences:
  • Explicitly, through a settings page or by asking the agent ("speak to me in Arabic").
  • Implicitly, by detecting preferences from conversations, then confirming them with the user before saving.
  • Using preferences: preferences are loaded at the start of each conversation and added to the agent's state. Language and tone are applied in the system prompt, while categories, price range, and brands are passed to the marketplace tools as filters.
  • Link to long-term memory: preferences can be stored as part of the long-term memory from Conversation Memory Management.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• User Profiles & Authentication, to link preferences to a user.
  • Conversation Memory Management, for long-term storage.
  • Marketplace tools that support filtering by price, brand, and category.

items.title: Risks
items.text:
• Wrong detected preferences: the agent may guess a preference incorrectly and keep using it.
  • Too narrow results: strict filters may hide good products the user would like.
  • Outdated preferences: users' budgets and interests change over time.

items.title: 7. Open Questions
items.text:
• Should preferences be managed from the website settings, from the chat, or both?
  • Should price range and brands be strict filters, or only used to rank results?
  • Which notifications are currently supported by GoCare?

items.title: 1. Feature Overview
items.text:
Visual Search allows GoCare users to upload an image and find similar products in the store, instead of searching by text when they don't know the product name.

The feature has three main parts:

  • Image upload: the user uploads a photo or screenshot from the search bar.
  • Visual product matching: a computer vision model compares the uploaded image with product images in the store.
  • Similar products results: the system shows the most visually similar in-stock products.

Example:

A user sees a lipstick shade she likes in a social media photo. She uploads the screenshot, and GoCare shows the closest lipstick shades available in the store.

items.title: 2. Current Website Status
items.text:
Based on the review in this report:

  • GoCare has a text search bar ("Search for products") on every page.
  • The store includes visual product categories such as makeup, perfumes, beauty devices, and gift sets.
  • There is no image-based search on the website currently.

What does this mean for the feature?

  • Visual Search can be added next to the existing search bar.
  • Product images already exist and can be used to build the image index.

items.title: 3. Business Objective
items.text:
The main goal is to help users find products they saw elsewhere, even when they don't know the name, and turn that interest into a purchase on GoCare.

Expected benefits:

  • Easier product discovery for users who don't know product names.
  • Higher conversion from social media inspiration to purchases.
  • A modern search experience that differentiates GoCare from competitors.
  • Fewer failed searches with no results.

Example:

Instead of typing "pink matte lipstick" and getting many unrelated results, the user uploads a photo and directly sees the closest matching shades.

Business Impact: High, according to the client's assessment.

items.title: 4.1 Questions for the Backend and Data Team
items.text:
1. Does every product have at least one clear, good-quality image?
  2. Are product images stored in a way that allows processing them in bulk?
  3. Is there existing infrastructure for running computer vision models (e.g. GPU or a cloud vision service)?
  4. Can the search backend support a new image-based search endpoint?
  5. Is product color or shade stored as structured data?

items.title: 5. Functional Requirements
items.text:
FR-01: Image upload

The system must allow users to upload an image or take a photo from the search bar.

FR-02: Visual product matching

The system must find store products that are visually similar to the uploaded image.

Example: an uploaded photo of a red perfume bottle returns perfumes with similar bottle shape and color.

FR-03: Similar products results

The system must show a list of similar, in-stock products, ordered by similarity.

FR-04: Filtering results

The user must be able to filter visual search results by category, price, or brand.

Proposed additional requirements (need client confirmation):

  • FR-05: Visual Search inside the chatbot.
  • FR-06: Cropping the uploaded image to focus on a specific product.
  • FR-07: Suggesting related products, such as products that complete the same look.

items.title: 6. Non-Functional Requirements
items.text:
1. Performance

Results must appear within a few seconds of uploading the image.

2. Accuracy

The most similar products must appear at the top of the results.

3. Scalability

The system must handle growth in the number of products and searches.

4. Privacy & Security

Uploaded images must be handled securely, not shared, and deleted when no longer needed, in line with data protection regulations in Saudi Arabia.

5. Reliability

If Visual Search fails, text search must keep working normally.

Note: target values for response time and search accuracy must be defined with the technical team.

items.title: 7. Data Requirements
items.text:
Data Purpose Status Product Images Build the visual search index Exists on the website; quality needs review Product Categories Filter and organize results Exists on the website Product Color / Shade Improve matching for makeup Unconfirmed Stock Availability Show only available products Unconfirmed Search Logs Measure and improve results Not collected yet for image search

Example:

If some products have low-quality images or images with busy backgrounds, the model may match them incorrectly, so product images must be reviewed first.

items.title: 8. Technical Feasibility
items.text:
The first version can be built using a pre-trained computer vision model:

  • Convert each product image into a numerical representation (image embedding).
  • Store the embeddings in a vector search index.
  • Convert the uploaded image the same way and find the closest product embeddings.

Later, improvements can be tested, such as:

  • Fine-tuning the model on GoCare's product images.
  • Combining image and text matching for better results.

Initial assessment: technically feasible using existing pre-trained models, provided that product images are of reasonable quality and infrastructure for running the model is available.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Good-quality product images.
  • Infrastructure for running the vision model and the vector search index.
  • Integration with the existing search bar on the website.
  • Collaboration between the Backend, Frontend, and Recommendation teams.

items.title: Constraints & Risks
items.text:
1. Image quality

User photos may be blurry, dark, or include many objects.

2. Similar-looking products

Many beauty products look alike, such as bottles of different perfumes.

3. Infrastructure cost

Running vision models may need extra computing resources.

4. Privacy

Uploaded images may include faces or personal information.

Example:

If a user uploads a selfie to find a lipstick shade, the system must focus on the lipstick color and must not store the user's face.

items.title: Meeting Decisions
items.text:
The following points were agreed in the meeting:

1. The feature is approved

The team has no objections to the Visual Search feature, and it can move forward as described in this page.

2. The feature is important

Visual Search is considered an important feature for GoCare, since it helps users find products they saw elsewhere, even when they do not know the product name.

3. All product categories are included

Visual Search covers all product categories, not only visual categories such as makeup and perfumes.

4. Visual Search appears in the search bar

Users access Visual Search from the existing search bar on the website.

5. Closest results when there is no exact match

If no similar product is found, the system shows the closest available results instead of an empty "no results" message.

6. Storing uploaded images depends on cost

Whether uploaded images are stored, or only used during the search, will be decided based on the storage cost.

7. "Similar" means the same shape and brand, and the same color for makeup

A product is considered similar to the uploaded image when it has the same shape and the same brand. For makeup products, such as lipstick, the color or shade is also used.

مثال:

مستخدمة ترى لون أحمر شفاه يعجبها في صورة على Instagram، لكنها لا تعرف اسمه.

  1. ترفع الصورة في شريط البحث في GoCare.
  2. يعرض لها GoCare أقرب درجات أحمر الشفاه المتوفرة في المتجر، فتشتري إحداها.
